sources.title: The Movies - Official Retail Manual (Steam app 7900)
sources.notes: QuarkXPress export dated 9/27/05; 22 PDF pages cover printed pages up to 43 (Customer Support); no Software License Agreement text present despite Contents listing p.48; entirely grayscale/monochrome halftone printing, no color evidence obtainable from images themselves, only from caption prose.

observations.situation: Main studio-lot HUD, printed p.5 ('Playing the Game / The In-Game Interface (HUD)')
observations.observation: A single labeled diagram over an empty, undeveloped dirt lot (no buildings/paths/people) shows: top-center scalloped tan banner with one star icon labeled 'Timeline'; top-left stacked labels 'Date, Pause, Play & Fast Forward' and 'Star Cards' pointing to a small vertical stack of ~3 tiny square portrait icons in the corner; top-right mirrored labels 'Cash Balance & Studio Ranking' and 'Movie Cards' pointing to a coin/rosette icon plus film-icon cluster; bottom-left single label 'Build Button' pointing to one icon. The whole screenshot sits in a beveled silver/chrome picture-frame border with a scallop tab top-center and round rivet studs at the four inner corners - the same frame chrome reused for every screenshot in the book. The lot is deliberately empty so nothing in the 3D world competes with the callouts.
observations.designLesson: A tutorial HUD diagram is clearest when the demoed world is emptied of content; the frame chrome itself is a single reusable motif applied to every image in the document.
observations.transfers: Use one consistent card/frame treatment for every UI screenshot/tooltip in your own style guide; for a first-run HUD-callout screen, show an empty/idle world state so labels aren't competing with gameplay clutter.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The specific gold-star/scallop Hollywood-pastiche motif is period flavor, not a HUD-legibility principle.

observations.situation: Timeline and time controls, printed p.5 caption text
observations.observation: Quoted: 'Timeline - The line along the top of the screen shows the passage of time from present day into the future, with each segment representing a year. Pay close attention: Events that affect your studio will be shown, such as new sets and facilities, award ceremonies, changes in public taste, gossip about your Stars and completion dates for research. Hold your mouse cursor over an icon to get more details.' And: 'Pause, Play and Fast Forward - Pause time, speed it up and play at normal speed. When you pause the game, you can still perform many tasks and check the status of your staff, studio and movies in production. You won't be able to pick up and drop items in the studio such as Stars, staff, movies or scripts when time is paused. When in Fast Forward mode, you can play the game as normal, except everything happens much faster.'
observations.designLesson: The timeline is a segmented year-per-tick strip that also hosts hoverable event icons (a second information layer riding on the same widget as time control).
observations.transfers: A top timeline strip can double as both a time-scrubber and an events ticker/notification rail without needing a separate notification tray.
observations.doesNotTransfer: n/a

observations.situation: Star Card sample, printed p.6-7
observations.observation: The illustrated Star Card is a tight head-and-shoulders portrait bust (young man in a flat cap) in the standard chrome-plaque frame, with a small numeral badge '31' in the top-left corner (a chart-rank number). No mood bar, hearts, or other iconography is drawn on the card itself in this sample image - all behavior is described only in the paragraph text, not shown as additional card furniture.
observations.designLesson: The card's visual payload is deliberately minimal (portrait + one rank numeral); richer state (mood, activity) is deferred to a hover tooltip rather than crammed onto the card face.
observations.transfers: Keep persistent roster/unit cards visually sparse (portrait + one primary numeral) and push secondary stats into on-demand hover/detail rather than icon-stacking the card.
observations.doesNotTransfer: n/a

observations.situation: Star Card interaction, printed p.6-7, quoted italic tip box
observations.observation: Quoted: 'Tip: To locate an actor, director or any of your staff, left-click on their card to jump to them on the studio lot. To pick up an actor, director or member of your staff to your current location, hold down the left mouse button on their card and drag them to the desired location.' Also: 'By using the buttons above the Star cards, you can cycle through your studio's other employees and quickly find the right person for a job.'
observations.designLesson: A roster card strip supports three distinct left-click gestures on the same card: click (camera jumps to them in the world), click-and-hold-then-release (teleports them to you), and separate cycle-arrows above the strip to page through the roster - all without opening a separate roster screen.
observations.transfers: For a persistent side-strip of unit/worker cards, supporting 'locate in world' (short click) and 'summon to my location' (click-hold-drag) as two weights of the same gesture keeps the roster fast to use without a modal list.
observations.doesNotTransfer: n/a

observations.situation: Movie Card status icons, printed p.6-7
observations.observation: Six discrete movie-card icon states are shown stacked vertically, each a small square icon in the chrome frame with a one-line caption to its right: (1) script/quill icon = 'scriptwriters busily working', (2) script-with-checkmark = 'script complete, ready for casting', (3) clapperboard/cast icon = 'casting complete, ready to shoot', (4) movie-camera icon = 'in the process of being filmed', (5) closed film-can icon = 'shot and ready for release', (6) glowing/starred film-can icon = 'released' (with a note that a pulsing $ sign appears over the card while it earns money). Below this, a horizontal row of 5 genre-icon tiles: Action (running/punching silhouette), Comedy (face with joke glasses), Horror (skull), Romance (two entwined figures), Sci-fi (robot/alien head with camera boom) - flat single-color pictograms on dark square tiles, one label word under each.
observations.designLesson: Movie production status is communicated purely through an icon swap on the same card slot (6 discrete states = 6 discrete icons), not a progress bar or percentage; genre is a separate always-visible badge in the card's corner using flat silhouette iconography.
observations.transfers: For a production-pipeline object (an order, a build job, a script), swapping a single glyph per discrete pipeline stage is more scannable at a glance across a grid of many cards than a percentage or bar; keep a fixed small icon set (5-6 genres here) as flat single-color silhouettes so they read at very small sizes.
observations.doesNotTransfer: This icon-swap approach only works because the pipeline has a small, fixed number of discrete stages (6); a pipeline with continuous/variable progress would need a different treatment (e.g., a fill bar) layered on top.

observations.situation: Post Production / Advanced Movie Maker editing HUD, printed p.26 'HUD Features'
observations.observation: A second, structurally different labeled diagram: a widescreen video-preview frame (playing a still of two actors, period dress, on a beach) in the same chrome-plaque frame, sitting above a full multi-track edit timeline. Left-edge label stack with leader lines to buttons running down the left side of the frame/timeline: Exit, Change Technology, Zooms, Expand Editing Options, Timeline, Scenes, Subtitle Track, Music Track, Sound Effect Track; below the frame: Dialogue Track, Timeline Slider, Player Controls (Play/Pause/Stop). Right-edge label stack: Current Scene (pointing at the frame itself), then a tight vertical button column - Tutorials, Audio Options, Fade In, Fade Out, Change Titles Style, Split Scene, Take Thumbnail, Trash Can, Save - then lower, Export Movie and Load. Timeline shown as thin horizontal lane bars of varying shades with small square/diamond keyframe markers, one lane per track type.
observations.designLesson: This editing mode intentionally abandons the 3D-lot HUD idiom (corner icons over a world view) for a flat desktop-NLE layout (stacked track lanes, scrubber, transport controls) - a completely different visual grammar for a completely different task (editing vs. management).
observations.transfers: When a game mode is conceptually a different tool (a video/level/blueprint editor nested inside a management sim), it's fine and often clearer to switch UI paradigms wholesale (adopt the paradigm users already know for that tool-type) rather than force-fit the main HUD's visual system onto it.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The dense vertical stack of ~9 small buttons down one edge is workable in a 1024x768-era manual screenshot but would need larger touch targets / grouping for a modern high-DPI or touch-friendly redesign.

observations.situation: Primary vs secondary click, printed p.10 table 'Item Being Used / Left-Click / Right-Click'
observations.observation: Verbatim table: Person -> Left-Click 'Pick Up/Drop', Right-Click 'Display all Information Bubbles'. Star Icon on HUD -> Left 'Select to Move/Drop', Right 'Display all Information Bubbles'. Movie Icon on HUD -> same pattern. Lot Ornaments -> Left 'Duplicate (into hand)', Right 'See Move Options'. Facilities -> Left 'Show Floorplan', Right '(none listed)'. Surrounding prose: 'click and hold the left mouse button to select and pick things up. Use the right mouse button to get information about the item your mouse cursor is over.'
observations.designLesson: Left-click = act/move/select, right-click = inspect/info, held uniformly across every clickable class except Facilities (which only supports one purpose: open floorplan).
observations.transfers: Commit to one binary left=act/right=inspect rule across every object class in a management-sim HUD; consistency here is what lets players transfer learned muscle memory from people to icons to props without re-learning per object type.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The one documented exception (Facilities having no right-click behavior) is presented as a real inconsistency in the source game, not a pattern to copy - a modern redesign should probably give Facilities a right-click info action rather than reproduce the gap.

observations.situation: Hover information-bubble system, printed p.8
observations.observation: Quoted: 'To display information about a Star, movie or building, simply hover the mouse cursor over an item and wait for the bubbles to appear' (hover delay stated qualitatively, no numeric duration given). 'Right-click on an item...All information pertaining to that item will be displayed instantly' (right-click = instant full version of the same hover system). 'Clicking on the central bubble closes all the attached bubbles. Moving the mouse cursor away from the item attached to the information bubbles also closes them' (bubbles form a radial cluster around one central hub bubble; dismiss by clicking the hub or moving away - no per-bubble close button). 'a bubble will display a red "!" symbol...or a blue "i" symbol' (two-tier severity badge language, reused across all subsystems). 'Many of the bars...represent a maximum and minimum value...Some of the bars have vertical lines marked on them known as "thresholds"...If a bar drops below the lower threshold...if a bar progresses past the upper threshold, you are managing your Star well' (bars carry baked-in threshold tick marks at gameplay-relevant breakpoints, not just a raw 0-100 fill). 'Guiding Streams and Star Trails - When you pick up a Star, script or a person from the queues, you'll see a trail of stars leading you to the most sensible action...This is only a suggestion, however...These also display on the Build menu, showing you which icons and options to select next.'
observations.designLesson: Five distinct information-affordance patterns bundled into one coherent system: (1) hover-delay tooltip, (2) right-click instant/full version of the same tooltip, (3) radial multi-bubble cluster with single-hub dismiss, (4) two-tier red/blue severity badges reused everywhere, (5) threshold-marked meter bars, plus a separate (6) diegetic breadcrumb-trail hint system that also highlights the relevant Build-menu icon.
observations.transfers: All six patterns transfer well to a modern 2D/isometric management HUD: hover-then-right-click-for-more as a two-speed info reveal; one hub bubble dismissing all its children; exactly two severity tiers reused everywhere (not three+); tick-marked meters instead of gradient-only bars; and an optional, ignorable in-world breadcrumb trail that also lights up the relevant menu icon.
observations.doesNotTransfer: No numeric hover delay is given, and the manual never actually shows bubbles/pips/trails rendered over live gameplay (only described in prose) - treat their exact visual appearance, color values, and timing as not verified from this source, only the behavior rules.

observations.situation: Build/construction menu, printed pp.6, 10-11, 16-17
observations.observation: 'The icon in the bottom left of the screen controls all construction...Click on this to see sub-menus: Facilities...Sets...Landscape and Ornaments' - a single bottom-left icon fans into exactly 3 categories, a flat two-level menu (not a deep tree). Facility placement: 'Place a stage school on your lot...the outline for which will be marked in yellow if it's OK to build and red if there's something obstructing the construction.' Builders then physically walk over and construct it (or appear instantly if 'Instantly Constructed Buildings' is toggled on in setup). Each facility in the Build > Facilities list is illustrated as an isolated hero-render building thumbnail on bare dirt with no surrounding lot context (catalog-style), e.g. Stage School = large white colonnaded mansion, Crew Facility = two-story house w/ porch, Casting Office = single-story cottage w/ double gable, Production Office = two-story manor w/ dormers, Script Office = cross-gabled cottage - all in the same chrome-plaque frame.
observations.designLesson: A single build button opening exactly 3 flat categories (not a deep menu tree) keeps construction shallow to navigate; placement legality is a binary yellow/red ghost outline; catalog thumbnails for buildable items are shown isolated on neutral ground, not in-context.
observations.transfers: Keep a build menu to a small, flat set of top-level categories; use a binary color-coded placement ghost (legal/illegal) rather than more granular feedback; show catalog/build-list thumbnails isolated on neutral backdrops so silhouette and material read clearly.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The manual never shows the build menu or placement ghost actually open over a populated lot - only isolated catalog renders and prose describe it, so the in-context appearance of the yellow/red ghost outline over a busy lot is not verified from this source.

observations.situation: Cash balance and studio ranking widgets, printed pp.6, 20-21
observations.observation: 'Cash Balance - Clicking on this figure takes you to the finance screen. Your Cash Balance contributes toward your ranking in the Charts.' Note: 'Your balance can go into the red but when you're in debt, you won't be able to build new sets or add certain facilities and lot ornamentation' (debt is a soft-lock on specific build categories, not a game-over). 'Studio Ranking - Clicking on the Studio Ranking icon in the top right corner of the screen takes you to the Charts screen.' Confirms the top-right HUD cluster (per the p.5 diagram) is dual-purpose: the cash number opens Finance, the adjacent rosette/rank icon opens Charts, in the same corner. Charts screen text: 'Left-click on the Studio Ranking rosette button...to open up the Star, Studio and Movie charts...Stars are highlighted to make them easier to find...left-click on the arrow button to the right of their name to scroll directly to the star rankings page...Right-click on their entry to view a breakdown.' A small accompanying thumbnail (low detail even at 110dpi) shows a two-pane layout: a left list of numbered rows with small icons, and a right pane with a large starburst graphic plus a row of small circular status icons at the bottom.
observations.designLesson: Two logically separate systems (money, competitive rank) share one physical HUD corner and one clickable cluster, differentiated only by which sub-element (number vs icon) is clicked; the Charts screen pairs a scrollable ranked list with a detail panel and its own right-click-for-breakdown affordance, mirroring the same left=navigate/right=inspect rule used everywhere else.
observations.transfers: Co-locating money and competitive-rank readouts in one HUD corner, with each element independently clickable to its own dedicated screen, keeps the corner compact without merging unrelated screens; reuse the same left=go-to-detail/right=inspect-breakdown rule inside sub-screens (e.g., a leaderboard), not just on the main HUD, for consistency.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The Charts thumbnail is too small/soft in this print source to reliably describe exact list density, typography, or icon meaning - confidence is MED and layout description should be treated as a rough sketch, not a precise spec.

observations.situation: Production pipeline and filming blockers, printed pp.12-13, 24-27
observations.observation: Documented pipeline in order: Script Office (hire writer, assign to a genre room, script pool) -> script complete -> Casting Office (drag the movie icon from the HUD into the office's floorplan; drop Stars/directors/extras/crew into role-rooms) -> drag movie icon into 'Shoot It' room to begin -> filming happens on a built Set -> Production Office (drag finished movie into 'Release' room; optionally drag the movie icon onto a marketing budget amount) -> Reviews room (drop a Star or the '!' icon in to see press/public opinion). Filming blocker: 'Information bubbles for a movie show you which sets a script will require. If a set is listed in red, there's an issue with that building - either it's in need of repair, you don't own it yet or another film is already shooting on it.' All three distinct causes collapse into one red-highlight signal; distinguishing which requires opening the info bubble.
observations.designLesson: A multi-stage production pipeline is entirely drag-and-drop between named 'rooms' inside facility floorplans (no dedicated dropdown/dialog screens for casting or scheduling); a single ambiguous red-highlight signal covers three different underlying blocker causes, resolved only by drilling into an info bubble.
observations.transfers: Modeling a production pipeline as drag targets into labeled sub-rooms of a facility (rather than modal dialogs) keeps everything spatial and consistent with the game's core object-manipulation language.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Collapsing three distinct blocker causes (repair needed / not owned / occupied) into one red color with no differentiation at the glance level is a usability gap in the source game, not a pattern worth reproducing - a modern redesign should differentiate blocker types visually (e.g., distinct icons) rather than copy this ambiguity.

observations.situation: Numeral badge convention on cards, printed pp.6-7
observations.observation: The Star Card sample shows a '31' numeral badge in its top-left corner; the manual states elsewhere 'The number on the card indicates your movie's current chart position' for Movie Cards - the same small-numeral-badge convention is applied to both Star and Movie cards, and in both cases it means global chart rank, never a quantity/count/level.
observations.designLesson: A numeral badge on a persistent card is used consistently for one meaning (global rank) across every card type in the game, never repurposed to mean something else (like stock count or level).
observations.transfers: If a HUD design puts a numeral badge on cards, keep its semantic meaning constant across every card type in the game so players never have to re-interpret it contextually.
observations.doesNotTransfer: A modern city-builder/management game that wants numeral badges to mean quantity/stock (a common convention in that genre) should choose a visually distinct badge shape from a rank badge, to avoid colliding with the convention this source establishes.

workflowsTraced.name: Building a facility and populating it (Hiring Builders -> Build Facilities -> staff it)

steps.whatHappens: Player hires Builders at the Staff Office by picking someone from a queue outside the gates and dropping them into the Create Builder room (documented-behavior: 'Pick someone up from the queue by left-clicking on them, and drop them into the Create Builder room by hovering over the staff office until the blue floorplan appears. Release them with a left-click.').

Player opens Build > Facilities, selects e.g. Stage School; a flat outline of the building follows the cursor, colored yellow if the location is legal and red if obstructed; player places it; hired Builders walk over and construct it (documented-behavior).

Once construction completes, a queue of talented hopefuls appears waiting outside; the player uses information bubbles to check talent/beauty/personality, then drags characters from the queue into the actor/director/extra rooms of the Stage School, adding them to the Star list on the left edge of the screen (documented-behavior).

workflowsTraced.name: Making and releasing a movie (Script -> Cast -> Shoot -> Release -> Review)

steps.whatHappens: Hire a scriptwriter, drag them into the desired genre room at the Script Office; they join the script pool and begin work (documented-behavior).

Build a Casting Office; drag the movie icon from the HUD's Movie Cards strip into the office's 'Begin Casting' room; the floorplan shows all roles (cast to crew); drop Stars/directors/extras/crew into the corresponding rooms (documented-behavior).

Once casting is complete, drag the movie icon into the 'Shoot It' room to begin filming; cast and crew assemble on the required Set (which must be built and unoccupied, or its card shows red) (documented-behavior).

After filming, drag the completed movie into the Production Office's Release room; optionally drag the movie icon onto a marketing-budget amount to set spend; release screens then show cost and Star impact (documented-behavior).

The Review screen shows press opinion of the finished film; the movie card's icon changes to a starred film-can, and a pulsing $ appears while it earns money at the box office (visible-in-still for the icon states, documented-behavior for the $ pulse).

workflowsTraced.name: Editing a finished film in Post Production

steps.whatHappens: Player drags a shot film into the Movie Player room of the Production Office (or loads a saved .trl file) to open the Post Production / HUD Features editing screen shown in the diagram: a video-preview frame above a multi-track timeline (Subtitle/Music/Sound Effect/Dialogue tracks) with edit buttons (Fade In/Out, Split Scene, Change Titles Style, Take Thumbnail) down the right edge (visible-in-still, per crop page14_hudfeatures_postprod.png).

Adding audio: click a track's timeline to add music/sound/dialogue from a drop-down list or browse the computer; dialogue can be recorded live via a Record button that becomes active only after clicking Play in this screen (documented-behavior).

Lip-sync: right-click a recorded dialogue track, choose which role/Star it maps to from a menu listing every role in the movie, click OK, then Play to watch the Star's lips move in time with the audio (documented-behavior, not shown as an actual animated sequence in this source).

original:manual.summary:
All 22 PDF pages of the retail manual (Steam app 7900, https://store.steampowered.com/manual/7900/) were rendered at 110dpi and viewed with Read. Printed page numbers run 2-43 across 11 spreads (PDF page N = printed pages roughly 2N-2/2N-1), confirmed against the corner star numerals and the internal QuarkXPress footer stamps visible on every page. The manual is grayscale halftone throughout, so no color values are verifiable from the images themselves - only from caption prose.

Key primary-source findings, each tied to a viewed page and (where applicable) a saved crop:

1. The one labeled HUD diagram (printed p.5, crop page03_hud_diagram.png) shows the main studio-lot interface as four corner clusters over a deliberately EMPTY lot: top-center Timeline banner, top-left Date/Pause/Play/Fast-Forward + Star Cards stack, top-right Cash Balance & Studio Ranking + Movie Cards stack, bottom-left single Build Button. Every screenshot in the book sits in an identical chrome-plaque picture-frame with a scallop-and-star top tab.
2. Star Cards (crop page04_starcard_v2.png) are tight portrait busts with a single rank-numeral badge ('31'); no other iconography is drawn on the card itself. Documented gestures: left-click jumps camera to the person, left-click-hold-drag relocates them to you, cycle-arrows above the strip page through the roster.
3. Movie Cards (crop page04_movie_and_genre.png) communicate production stage purely via a 6-state icon swap (script quill -> checked script -> clapperboard -> camera -> closed film can -> glowing film can with pulsing $ once released), plus a fixed 5-icon genre badge row (Action/Comedy/Horror/Romance/Sci-fi) shown as flat single-color silhouettes.
4. A second, structurally distinct labeled diagram exists for Post Production (printed p.26, crop page14_hudfeatures_postprod.png): a video-preview frame over a full multi-track timeline (Subtitle/Music/Sound Effect/Dialogue lanes) with ~9 small edit buttons stacked down each side (Fade In/Out, Split Scene, Take Thumbnail, Trash Can, Save, Export, Load, etc.) - a desktop-NLE visual language, deliberately different from the 3D-lot HUD.
5. A verbatim click-behavior table (printed p.10) fixes left-click=act/move/select and right-click=inspect/info uniformly across People, Star-icon-on-HUD, Movie-icon-on-HUD, and Lot Ornaments; Facilities are the one documented exception (left-click only, opens floorplan).
6. The hover/info-bubble system (printed p.8) is fully documented: hover-then-wait for a bubble, right-click for the instant full version, bubbles form a radial cluster dismissed via one central hub, a two-tier red-'!'/blue-'i' severity badge language reused everywhere, threshold-tick-marked meter bars (not raw fills), and a separate diegetic 'guiding streams/Star trails' breadcrumb hint system that also highlights the relevant Build-menu icon.
7. Build menu is a single bottom-left icon fanning into exactly 3 flat categories (Facilities/Sets/Landscape&Ornaments); placement uses a binary yellow=legal/red=obstructed ghost outline; every buildable facility is illustrated as an isolated catalog-style hero render on bare dirt.
8. Cash Balance and Studio Ranking share one HUD corner but open two different screens (Finance vs Charts) depending on which sub-element is clicked; going into debt soft-locks specific build categories rather than ending the game.
9. The full script->cast->shoot->release->review production pipeline is documented as pure drag-and-drop between named rooms inside facility floorplans; a filming blocker (a set shown in red) collapses three distinct causes (needs repair / not owned / occupied by another shoot) into one ambiguous signal, resolved only via the info bubble.

Nothing in this source shows an actual animated hover/click transition or a populated (non-empty) main HUD screenshot - both are explicitly flagged as unverified/not-shown-in-this-source. All observations, a printed-vs-PDF page map, design lessons (what transfers / doesn't) for each finding, and three traced workflows (build-a-facility, make-and-release-a-movie, edit-in-post-production) are included in full above. All rendered pages are saved at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-bruce/41c841f9-0429-4923-8623-96050aba6653/scratchpad/research/manual/pages/page-01.png through page-22.png, and the four interface-diagram crops are saved under .../research/manual/crops/ (page03_hud_diagram.png, page04_starcard_v2.png, page04_movie_and_genre.png, page14_hudfeatures_postprod.png). A brief REPORT.md pointer file was also saved to the output folder (a Write-tool-based full report file was blocked by this session's file-output policy, so the complete findings live in this response rather than in that file).

original:footage.summary:
Per harness instructions, no REPORT.md file was written — all findings are inline below. Output folder (frames + contact sheets only; source videos deleted after extraction) is at the path in reportFile.

Downloaded and sampled 3 unedited, full-quality YouTube "Let's Play"/gameplay-capture videos of The Movies (2005, base game, PC), all with unobstructed UI and no webcam overlay: V1 "The Movies - Ep. 1 - Movie Studio Tycoon" (PHENIXX BUILDS, 2020-03-28, 35min), V2 "Lets Play Classics - The Movies on PC" (Monkiedude22, 2017-01-31, 79min), V3 "The Movies (2005) - Gameplay [1080p60FPS]" (Mausser, 2024-12-31, 25min, played at in-game Fast-Forward throughout). yt-dlp required `--js-runtimes node --extractor-args "youtube:player_client=android" -f 18` to work around 403s from the default web/ios/tv clients (PO-token issue); noting this as a reusable fix.

Traced three continuous workflows with 8-15 timestamped frames each: (A) construction catalogue → drag-placement (red-invalid → hazard-taped-valid, a genuinely confirmed 6-frame drag sequence) → scaffold → finished building; (B) script "shooting schedule" quill/popup → scene-level progress ("Scene 3/3") → a live blocker state (red negative cash + red flag on an understaffed casting zone) → "Released!" card → the finished b&w film literally playing back in video-player chrome → in-universe credits; (C) world-space hire/fire zone panels and a genre/category cycling strip (5-cell grid, cells swap content and highlight-color on selection) plus casting-panel role slots with a red blocker badge. Also captured: empty studio, mature lot, multiple hover tooltips (verbatim tutorial/flavor text), StarMaker actor-creation attribute sheets (closest analog found to a "person detail card," but pre-hire not post-hire), and a "Studio Charts" competitor leaderboard as the finance/management view.

Two things flagged as genuinely unresolved rather than guessed at: (1) V1 and V2 show two different release-summary layouts (numeric stars+critic-quote cards vs. plain word-grades) and it's unclear from footage alone whether that's a version/difficulty/DLC difference; (2) no right-click context menu and no post-hire personnel-inspection panel were found in ~2 hours of combined sampled footage — both classed not-verified rather than assumed absent.

workflowsTraced.name: Construction: catalogue -> drag-placement -> validity feedback -> scaffold -> finished building

steps.whatHappens: Main menu mid-transition (blue/purple particle wipe), confirms this is a rendered animated transition, not a static menu.
Create Your Studio modal: two mannequins flank a card with logo-cycle arrows, Studio Name / Name fields, Skip Tutorial checkbox.
Baseline empty lot: bare dirt/grass, one foundation outline, full HUD already present (date, cash $148,635, landscape-tool swatches) despite nothing built.
Facilities catalogue dropdown open over bare ground: 8 priced rows with owned-counts.
A red-outlined building footprint (rotate-icon glyph at center) appears next to an existing house — placement preview begins, invalid (red).
Same footprint has moved and rotated versus the previous frame, still red/invalid — confirms the outline is live-tracking a drag, not a fixed animation.
Footprint now bounded by yellow/black hazard tape at a settled position = accepted placement; cash ticking down in small increments each frame ($128,819->811).
Hazard-taped footprint holds steady across two more frames = site confirmed and queued for construction.
A separate, older building elsewhere on the lot: full timber scaffold + blue tarp shell, two worker figures crossing the yard, a flagged pole near the entrance.
Same scaffold now has a black tarp cap over the roof ridge (topping-out stage) plus two small ground pixel-icon markers that weren't there before.
Two buildings now stand fully finished (a two-story house, a large colonnaded building) with workers walking paved paths between them.
A single large terracotta-roofed office building fully built with a guard booth and road traffic — lot now reads as a working studio.

workflowsTraced.name: Script -> shoot (with schedule + blocker) -> release -> watch the film -> credits

steps.whatHappens: Small wood-shed stage building with a white feather-quill icon floating above it in a speech-bubble anchor; tutorial caption: 'It's first scene is now being shot.'
The bubble expands into a full 'Shooting Schedule' popup: 'Currently Shooting: Comedy' with a progress bar; tutorial text explains left-click to continue.
Same popup now labeled 'Fast Forward' at top — a different sub-control being hovered within the same world-space widget.
Wide shot: a new mansion has appeared near the stage shed; a decoration hover tooltip reads 'Pretty Circular Flowerbed: $120...'.
A live shooting-status popup shows scene-level granularity not seen in V1/V2: 'Currently Shooting' + a second tooltip 'Where's Baby? Assembling On Set... Scene 3/3' plus a Cast & Crew list.
Blocker state: casting zone panel shows 'Extras 1/1' with a red flag/pin planted on that zone, and the cash HUD reads red/negative ($-7,388) at the same moment.
'Released!' card for 'The Baggage Boy': Script Quality stars, Director/Starring credits, three qualitative outcome rows (Star Relationships: AVERAGE, Repair of Sets: AWFUL, Crew Experience: AWFUL).
Cuts to a black screen in-universe vanity card ('Dude22 Studios / Production') inside a framed video-player chrome with a scrubber and play/pause icons.

B&W footage plays: a man walks between, then lifts, a barbell prop on a porch set, with in-video timestamps overlaid (00:26:10 -> 01:08:00), confirming a real scripted playback rather than one static image.
End-card disclaimer ('All events and characters in this movie are fictitious...') plus fake production-company logos PICOVISION / MONOHUE.

workflowsTraced.name: Hire/staff: world-space zone panel -> roster list -> genre/category cycling strip

steps.whatHappens: Ground overlaid with large translucent blue diagonal-striped polygons labeled 'Create Director' and 'Fire'; two round numbered staff-portrait thumbnails stacked as a mini roster list; two NPCs stand at a sign-board between the zones.
A 5-cell blue grid labeled by genre (Horror, Sci-Fi, Fire, Action, Comedy) appears — the staff/category cycling strip.
Same 5-cell layout, but one cell now reads 'Script Pool' (pale-green tint) in place of a genre slot — cell content is contextual, not fixed.
Same grid, 'Script Pool' cell now solid green (selected/active state) among the remaining genre cells.
Casting-zone panel reading 'Director / Lead Roles / Crew 2/2 / Extras 1/1 / Shoot It' with a small red circular badge overlaid on the Director cell (unfilled-role blocker).
Same panel family elsewhere shows 'Begin Casting' rendered as a discrete button, plus 4 numbered staff portraits each with a thin green bar underneath, stacked screen-left.
StarMaker 'Advanced Mode': rotating 3D head preview plus a column of small angle/dial icons, one per adjustable facial region.

Full 'Bob Smith' attribute sheet: portrait plus ~13 labeled sliders (Looks, Trimness, Chest Size, Action, Comedy, Romance, Horror, Sci-Fi, Western, Boredom, Stress, Mood, Fear/Lower) — closest analog found to a person-detail card, but pre-hire/creation-time.

observations.situation: World-space hire/fire and genre-category panels rendered directly on the ground plane during casting/hiring at ~20:00-30:10
observations.observation: Contextual menus (hire/fire, genre-category picker) are flat translucent skewed polygons textured onto the terrain mesh itself, matching ground perspective, rather than screen-space cards.
observations.designLesson: Binding a menu's geometry to the physical location it affects keeps the player's attention anchored to 'this office, right here' rather than abstracting the action into a menu bar.
observations.transfers: The principle — bind the UI to its physical target (e.g. a glowing build-slot on the exact tile) — transfers well to a modern isometric HUD.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The literal full-perspective skewed-quad rendering is expensive, showed z-fighting/occlusion against terrain detail in this footage, and reads as visually dated; a modern HUD should achieve the same anchoring with a docked panel plus a connecting highlight/beam to the world tile instead.

observations.situation: A building footprint being dragged into place, 6 frames over ~10 seconds (8:56-9:06)
observations.observation: Placement validity is communicated purely by a hue swap: red outline while invalid/mid-drag, then yellow-black hazard tape once a valid site is confirmed — no icon or text is needed.
observations.designLesson: A strong, high-contrast binary color code for valid/invalid drag state reads instantly even at small preview size, with zero extra UI chrome.
observations.transfers: Directly — red/invalid vs. affirmative/valid outline color-coding is a proven, low-cost pattern for any grid- or footprint-based placement tool in a modern 2D/isometric builder.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The specific hazard-tape texture for 'confirmed' is a period/construction-realism skin; a modern HUD should keep the color logic but re-skin the confirmed state (soft glow, dashed-to-solid border) rather than copy the tape motif.

observations.situation: Same blue zone-panel widget reused across hire (20:00), fire (20:00), and genre/category selection (23:40-30:10)
observations.observation: One flexible container widget (translucent blue diagonal-striped polygon + bold label) is reskinned by label text alone to serve hiring, firing, and category-picking, and its cell contents can swap (e.g. a genre cell becoming 'Script Pool').
observations.designLesson: Building one flexible chip/zone component that many features share minimizes the number of distinct UI systems a player must learn.
observations.transfers: The economy-of-widgets approach transfers strongly to any HUD with many small categorical choices — reuse one component, vary its content, rather than bespoke UI per feature.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Relying on label text alone to distinguish a constructive action (hire) from a destructive one (fire) from a neutral one (pick a genre) is a legibility risk at a glance — the footage never shows 'Fire' colored red/danger despite being the destructive action; a modern version should differentiate stakes with color/icon, not text alone.

observations.situation: Shooting-schedule popup hovered at 24:00-24:40, tutorial copy visible verbatim on-screen
observations.observation: In-context tooltips double as the tutorial system: the shooting-schedule bubble carries full instructional sentences ('Scenes that are still to be shot are displayed in the Movie's Shooting Schedule bubble... Left-click on this bubble to continue.') rather than deferring to a separate help screen.
observations.designLesson: Teaching the UI through the UI itself, in-context and at the moment of relevance, avoids a separate onboarding modal stack.
observations.transfers: Just-in-time contextual tutorial copy attached to the exact control it explains is a durable, genre-agnostic pattern worth keeping.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The sheer sentence-length of these bubbles (3+ full sentences) competes for space with the gameplay scene behind it in this 2005 layout; a modern widescreen HUD has room to dock this copy in a side panel instead of overlaying the world.

observations.situation: A casting zone panel showing 'Extras 1/1' at the same moment the cash HUD reads negative
observations.observation: Blocked/problem states are shown ambiently — a small red flag/pin planted on the understaffed zone plus the persistent cash counter recoloring to red for a deficit — rather than through a dedicated alerts panel or modal warning.
observations.designLesson: Recoloring an already-visible persistent stat (cash) or a small in-place badge (the flag) to flag trouble is cheap and avoids interrupting flow with modal alerts for routine shortfalls.
observations.transfers: The low-friction ambient-recolor approach for common/recoverable problems transfers well to a modern minimal HUD.
observations.doesNotTransfer: No consolidated alerts list or notification center was observed anywhere across ~2 hours of combined footage, so a player not looking directly at the affected zone could plausibly miss the problem; a modern equivalent should pair ambient recoloring with a small persistent problem-count badge (inference: no footage actually showed a miss, but no aggregation UI was ever seen either).

observations.situation: Post-release: 'Released!' card at 26:40, then video-player chrome plays the finished film 27:00-28:20, ending on a disclaimer/credits card
observations.observation: The finished movie is not just a stat summary — it plays back inside literal video-player chrome (scrubber, play/pause), opening on an in-universe production-company vanity card and closing on a fictitious disclaimer plus fake company logos (PICOVISION, MONOHUE).
observations.designLesson: Letting the player watch the artifact they made, framed exactly like a real film with its own presentation chrome, is a strong payoff/reward loop specific to a creation-management sim.
observations.transfers: Surfacing the player's output as a first-class, in-fiction artifact (not just a stat delta) transfers to any creation-management game.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The specific b&w silent-film pastiche and multi-minute full playback mode are period/genre-specific and pacing-heavy; a modern isometric studio game would more likely surface this as a poster/trailer card or short animated vignette to respect current pacing expectations.

observations.situation: Release-summary screens compared: V1's numeric card at 31:40-33:00 vs. V2's word-grade card at 26:40
observations.observation: Two different release-summary layouts were found across the two sessions — V1 shows Script Quality stars plus a 'Movie Quality' panel with critic pull-quote cards from four named outlets (filmfilm, RMN, FilmXX, The Reporter), while V2 shows plain qualitative word-grades (AVERAGE/AWFUL) with no critic quotes.
observations.designLesson: If a game ships more than one results-screen variant (by version, difficulty, or DLC), make sure both are reachable and legible, or consolidate to one canonical results screen for the core loop.
observations.transfers: The idea of a rich, multi-source critical-reception screen (quoted reviews from distinct 'outlets') as post-release feedback transfers well to any creation-sim final-score screen.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Not resolved from footage alone which build/setting produces which layout — flagged as unverified rather than a transferable lesson in itself.

unverified: A dedicated post-hire personnel inspection panel (click a staff member standing on the lot to see a persistent stat card) was not located in ~2 hours of combined sampled footage; closest analogs found were the pre-hire StarMaker attribute sheet and small roster portrait+bar rows inside casting panels.
Right-click context-menu behavior — no frame across all three videos showed a distinguishable right-click action or resulting menu distinct from left-click/hover tooltips.

The exact cause of the two different release-summary layouts (V1 numeric stars + critic-quote cards vs. V2 plain word-grades) — could be a version/patch difference, a difficulty/settings toggle, or base game vs. an expansion state; V1's splash art carries Stunts & Effects branding despite a base-game-shaped main menu, so the build delta could not be pinned down from footage alone.

Audio cues and UI sound design were not checked at all — no audio playback capability was available in this environment; all 'transition'/'animation' claims above come from visual diffing of consecutive extracted frames only.
blocked: Initial yt-dlp downloads returned HTTP 403 from the default (web/ios/tv/android_vr) YouTube extraction clients; resolved by adding --js-runtimes node --extractor-args "youtube:player_client=android" -f 18, which worked for all three videos. Not a lasting blocker, but noted in case it recurs for future footage-gathering tasks.

original:stills.summary: Viewed 33 distinct primary-source images across 4 collections, all saved under /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-bruce/41c841f9-0429-4923-8623-96050aba6653/scratchpad/research/stills/: (1) all 15 official Steam store screenshots for The Movies, app 7900, pulled full-size (1024x768/1275x975) via the Steam appdetails API and viewed — steam/steam_ss_01..15.jpg; (2) 9 original-2005 MobyGames retail screenshots recovered via Wayback Machine (EXIF-dated Oct 2005, Adobe Photoshop CS-edited), 160x120 thumbnails upscaled with ffmpeg for legibility — moby/moby_thumb_0X(_big).{jpg,png}; (3) 4 GameSpot review screenshots at full 1024x768 with their original figcaptions recovered — gamespot/gs_01..04.jpg; (4) 10 Steam screenshots for the Stunts & Effects expansion (app 7910), 4 viewed closely and confirmed to be UI-free posed marketing renders (one has a baked-in logo lockup proving it's not a raw capture) — stunts/stunts_0X.jpg. Coverage successfully hit: top HUD (date/cash/star-level/VCR transport), left staff-portrait rail (mood-bar + status-icon cards, no name label), a mirrored right-side task/alert icon rail, world-anchored speech-bubble/thought-bubble callouts used for both people (mood, dialogue) and buildings (progress, hover-name), a full-lot color-zoning overlay mode, a post-production filmstrip/editing-timeline screen, and a distinct 2D-illustrated awards-ceremony screen. Coverage NOT achieved despite being requested: no working screenshot of a literal casting-office interior UI, script-writing screen, finance/ledger screen, or build-catalogue item-picker — MobyGames' individual screenshot pages and the-movies-game.fandom.com (Script_Office/Casting_Office/Custom_Scriptwriting_Office pages, which describe but whose embedded images could not be fetched) were Cloudflare-gated against curl/WebFetch even through Wayback replay; IGN/Eurogamer/PC Gamer review pages were leads only, not fetched, within the time budget. All Stunts & Effects images viewed are confirmed marketing renders, not gameplay captures, so they add no new UI evidence beyond confirming a distinct saturated-blue soundstage "set type" for VFX compositing.

observations.situation: Every gameplay screenshot across S1 (12/15) and S3 (4/4) — the only exceptions are 3 UI-free cinematic wides in S1 and all 4 Stunts & Effects marketing renders in S4.
observations.observation: A persistent ~30-36px dark top HUD bar (≈4% of a 768px-tall frame) spans the full screen width, holding left-to-right: a rounded date pill with a masks icon (e.g. 'Jun 1994','Oct 1929'), a horizontal timeline strip with small colored dot event-markers, VCR-style rewind/pause/play/fast-forward transport buttons (observed in a pressed/hand-cursor-hover state in steam_ss_08.jpg), then right-aligned a rounded cash pill ($ amount) and a circular numbered star-level badge (values 1-10 seen across the corpus) ringed by small gold/outline stars as a to-next-level meter.
observations.designLesson: Date/time, cash, and a prestige meter are fused into one bar whose position never moves across 20+ in-fiction years or any zoom level — total spatial orientation without a minimap.
observations.transfers: A single fixed top strip binding clock+money+prestige-meter is a durable, still-current HUD pattern for a tycoon/management game.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Literal VCR transport buttons (rewind/pause/play/ff) read as dated; a modern HUD should fold time-control into a speed toggle rather than four physical transport icons.

observations.situation: Left edge of the frame in most populated gameplay shots: steam_ss_02,03,04,06,07,08,09,10,11,12,14 and gamespot gs_01..04.
observations.observation: A vertical rail of ~60-64px-wide (~6% of 1024px width) portrait cards sits flush against the left screen edge, count varying 3-7 per scene (not a fixed roster length). Each card = a naturalistic front-facing headshot photo-portrait, a thin color-filled horizontal bar underneath (green/yellow/orange/red, read as mood/energy) and a small corner badge icon: a lightning bolt (available/energetic) in most cards or a 'Zzz' glyph (off-duty/asleep) in others (steam_ss_05.jpg, steam_ss_09.jpg, steam_ss_10.jpg). No name text appears on any rail card in any viewed still — identity is conveyed by portrait alone; small numbers overlaid on some cards (e.g. '44','42','39') read as character age given they change alongside visibly different apparent ages, not a roster index.
observations.locator: flush left edge, full card stack top-to-bottom starting under the top HUD
observations.designLesson: The rail is a live, scene-filtered 'who is relevant right now' list, not a full roster browser — count and members change per shot.
observations.transfers: Portrait + single color status bar + one corner status icon is a legible, low-chrome pattern for at-a-glance status of people relevant to the current view.
observations.doesNotTransfer: No name label on the card is a real usability gap by modern standards — a remake should add a name-on-hover or micro name strip.

observations.situation: Right edge of frame, same shots that show the left staff rail: steam_ss_02,03,04,06,07,08,09,10,12 and gamespot gs_01,gs_03.
observations.observation: A second vertical rail, same ~60px width, mirrors the staff rail on the opposite edge but holds task/alert icon tiles instead of portraits: circular 'i' info-bubble, checkmark-on-clipboard, thought-cloud, skull (danger/hazard — present in every VFX/hazard-adjacent shot such as steam_ss_07.jpg's robot-suit filming and steam_ss_09.jpg's basketball court), dollar-sign-in-star, and paper-with-pencil (script/writing task, seen in steam_ss_04.jpg and steam_ss_11.jpg). 2-5 of these appear per shot from an apparent fixed icon vocabulary of ~6-8 types.
observations.locator: flush right edge, mirrored vertical position to the staff rail
observations.designLesson: The UI deliberately balances the screen: a person-rail on the left is mirrored by a task/alert-rail on the right at identical width/position, keeping the 3D viewport visually centered rather than lopsided.
observations.transfers: Symmetric flanking rails (people left, tasks/system right) at equal width is a clean, screen-balanced convention worth reusing.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Icon-only tiles with no visible text label force memorizing a small icon language; a modern HUD should add a hover tooltip even if the original may or may not have had one (not verifiable from a still).

observations.situation: Character- and building-focused shots: steam_ss_12.jpg (Dave Woods on set), gamespot gs_01.jpg (Peter Molyneux NPC cameo), steam_ss_10.jpg (two seated characters at a restaurant).
observations.observation: Selection/status information is shown as floating comic-style speech- or thought-bubbles anchored in 3D world-space directly above a character's head, not as a docked 2D side panel. steam_ss_12.jpg shows a bordered bubble 'Dave Woods / Movie: Dogbiter & Fitch / On set.' stacked above a separate pink oval 'Addictions / Food: [bar]' bubble. gamespot gs_01.jpg shows a yellow 'Work / Stress: [bar]' bubble above a gray-blue bubble naming 'Peter Molyneux' (a real Lionhead-founder in-joke NPC) with his current movie and a 'Wanting a chat' line. steam_ss_10.jpg shows two overlapping word-balloons with full first-person interior-monologue sentences ('I like her but I feel so awkward here...' / 'It's too soon to be somewhere this intimate with him...') each with a tail pointing to one of two seated characters.
observations.designLesson: Information is pinned to world-space above its subject (diegetic callouts) rather than pulled into a fixed 2D side panel, keeping the lot itself the primary screen.
observations.transfers: World-anchored contextual callouts (mood/task/relationship-thought) are a strong, still-fresh idiom for keeping players watching the world rather than tabbing to a menu.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Hand-drawn comic-style word balloons carrying full prose sentences read as very 2005/Sims-era twee; a modern equivalent should favor terser icon+one-line text.

observations.situation: steam_ss_11.jpg (full-lot zoning view), gamespot gs_04.jpg (building hover-label), gamespot gs_02.jpg (lot overview with multiple callouts).
observations.observation: Two distinct affordances for lot legibility: (a) steam_ss_11.jpg shows a toggled 'planning mode' where the whole lot is tinted with large semi-transparent colored zone regions labeled in italic script laid on the ground plane — 'Fire' (green), 'Cult Packs' (gray/blue diagonal), 'Mainstream Packs' (blue diagonal), 'Movie-making' (red/white diagonal), with a 'Stars & Studio' sub-region, small yellow warning triangles at boundaries, viewed from the same raised 3/4 camera as normal play (not a flat orthographic map). (b) gamespot gs_04.jpg shows ordinary gameplay camera with a plain rounded-rect tooltip 'Casting Office' hovering beside a large Mediterranean-style gated building — confirms building ID is a lightweight hover-label, not a separate legend/map screen. (c) gamespot gs_02.jpg (same camera style, zoomed/panned) shows 4 simultaneous stacked yellow-green callouts with progress bars ('Practicing Romance / Progress' x2, 'Rehab Progress', 'Stage School') each with a stem pointing to a specific building, i.e. multiple concurrent background activities surfaced at once across the whole lot.
observations.locator: steam_ss_11 = full-frame overlay; gs_04 = tooltip beside building; gs_02 = 4 callouts across visible lot
observations.designLesson: A full-screen semantic zoning wash is reserved for a distinct toggle mode, while everyday building identification is a lightweight hover tooltip in the ordinary camera — two different affordances for two different questions.
observations.transfers: A toggleable full-lot color-zone overlay (SimCity-style) is a high-value pattern for a modern isometric studio-management HUD to show genre/audience zoning at a glance.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Multiple simultaneous free-floating progress callouts (gs_02 shows 4 at once) risk clutter at larger lot sizes; a modern HUD should collapse these into a summary list or gate them to hover/select.

observations.situation: moby_thumb_01 (upscaled): a street scene with a car and pedestrians, top HUD reading 'Now Recording', with a two-row filmstrip editing bar occupying the bottom third of frame.
observations.observation: A distinct post-production screen type absent from the Steam/GameSpot sets: below the normal 3D shot sits a dark horizontal timeline with a scrubber bar and two stacked rows of small square clip thumbnails (row 1: ~4 thumbnails plus an empty 'x'-marked slot; row 2: ~4 more, one bright red/orange suggesting a flagged clip), flanked left/right by small round icon buttons (gear/settings-style).
observations.locator: bottom third of frame, two-row filmstrip
observations.designLesson: Post-production is modeled as a two-row filmstrip/editing-bench bolted onto the bottom of the same live 3D viewport used for filming, rather than cutting away to an abstract edit-list screen.
observations.transfers: A persistent bottom filmstrip with orderable clip thumbnails is a legible metaphor worth reusing for an in-fiction editing screen.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Cramming a full two-row NLE-style timeline into the bottom third of an otherwise live 3D viewport (rather than a dedicated full-screen editor) is hard to read even at native res — borderline illegible at this thumbnail's native 160x120 despite 4x upscale — a modern UI should give editing its own full-screen mode.

observations.situation: moby_thumb_05,06,07,09 (upscaled) — 4 near-identical states of one screen with different presenter figures.
observations.observation: A fully separate non-3D-viewport screen: a masthead reads 'The [??]Reporter Presents' above a bold title 'Los premios Libertad de oro' (Spanish-localized build). A translucent glass-panel lists ~8 award category rows each with a small colored genre icon, some rows highlighted in a warm-yellow band with trophy-outline glyphs. Below, two FLAT 2D illustrated presenter figures in formalwear stand at a podium against a glowing blue spotlight backdrop (a different art style from the game's normal 3D character models), with a word-balloon dialogue caption box lower-left and a row of ~9 small diamond/gem icons along the bottom edge. Presenter hair/skin/outfit differs across the 4 frames, confirming a randomized presenter pair per ceremony rather than one fixed pair.
observations.designLesson: The one non-3D 'spectacle' screen in the game switches art style entirely (flat 2D illustration vs. the game's normal 3D), a deliberate register-shift signalling a theatrical/ceremonial moment.
observations.transfers: Reserving a distinct non-diegetic full-screen treatment (glossy frame, trophy iconography, different visual register) for the awards payoff moment is a good beat to preserve.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The flat-2D presenter art clashes with the polished 3D game around it in a way that reads as a budget/scope seam rather than an intentional choice — a modern equivalent should keep one consistent render style (e.g., same 3D engine with a formal camera+lighting setup) instead of swapping to illustration.

observations.situation: Filming scenes across steam_ss_02,03,04,07,08 and gamespot gs_01,gs_03.
observations.observation: Filming scenes consistently cluster 4-7 crew figures around one practical camera prop — an old wood-and-bellows box camera for the 1920s scene (steam_ss_04.jpg), a modern shoulder-rig camera with boom mic in steam_ss_08.jpg, a wheeled tripod camera during the VFX robot-suit shoot in steam_ss_07.jpg. Crew wear a visually identical grey-denim-overalls-over-collared-shirt uniform across every in-fiction era shown (1929 through 2015 in the corpus), while principal cast costume visibly changes with era (1929 flapper dresses in steam_ss_04 vs. 1982 mod skirt-and-knee-socks in steam_ss_10).
observations.locator: on-set crowd around the camera prop
observations.designLesson: Costuming is used as a fast, silent read of both role and era — a timeless crew uniform lets 'crew' register instantly while principal-cast clothing is the visible era marker.
observations.transfers: A stable crew-uniform silhouette that never changes lets players parse crew-vs-talent instantly in a busy shot even at small isometric sprite scale.
observations.doesNotTransfer: None — this pattern is sound and era-agnostic.

observations.situation: Early lot: steam_ss_04.jpg (Oct 1929, level 3). Mature/dense lot: steam_ss_13.jpg, steam_ss_14.jpg, steam_ss_15.jpg (no HUD, hero cinematic angles).
observations.observation: steam_ss_04.jpg shows a small, sparse lot: one wood-framed open-air stage set, a single scaffold tower, a few palm trees, one modest cream building and a small red-tile-roof structure, with wide empty lawn. steam_ss_13/14/15.jpg show a visually dense, city-block-scale lot: multi-story brick apartment-style blocks, Art-Deco cream facades, a factory building with smokestacks in the distance, a beach, an ornate entrance gate flanked by tall star-topped stone pylons, dozens of pedestrian NPCs, multiple trailers/campers, and 2-3 raw plywood/scaffold set walls under simultaneous construction.
observations.designLesson: Studio progression is communicated almost entirely through lot density and architectural variety rather than an abstract HUD number — the star-badge is the only numeric confirmation, everything else is read off the world.
observations.transfers: Using world density/variety as the primary progression signal (over an abstract progress bar) is a strong pattern for a spiritual successor's isometric lot.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The late-game screenshots are lit as glossy 'hero' marketing renders (very saturated, soft-shadowed, no HUD) that likely oversell real-time density vs. normal play — treat as aspirational framing, not typical captured gameplay.

observations.situation: stunts_02.jpg (blue-screen soundstage compositing a toy jet), stunts_03.jpg (car wheelie/crash stunt), stunts_06.jpg (fire/explosion compositing vignette), stunts_10.jpg (stuntman diving toward a crash pad, with a baked-in 'The MOVIES / STUNTMAN — THE MOVIES: STUNTS & EFFECTS' logo lockup proving this is a posed marketing render, not a raw capture).
observations.observation: All 4 closely-viewed Stunts & Effects screenshots show zero HUD chrome (no top bar, no rails, no callouts) — confirmed marketing renders rather than gameplay captures. Content documents a distinct saturated-blue soundstage set type for VFX compositing (visible lighting truss + scaffold frame + solid blue cyc wall, contrasted with the practical day-lit sets in the base-game corpus) and stunt-choreography setpieces (marked crash pad with cones/hurdles, car crash physics with a flipping vehicle).
observations.designLesson: From this evidence alone, the Stunts & Effects expansion's marketing leaned on cinematic stunt/VFX vignettes rather than showcasing new HUD screens — it reads as a content/verb expansion layered onto an unchanged base UI, not a UI overhaul.
observations.transfers: The blue-screen soundstage as a distinct, saturated-color 'set type' room is a good world/set-variety idea to carry forward.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Not applicable — no UI shown to evaluate for transfer.

unverified: A literal casting-office interior UI, script-writing/text-entry screen, finance/ledger screen, or build-catalogue item-picker grid were requested targets but no working screenshot of any of them was found or viewed in this lens; the closest verified equivalents are the zoning overlay and the building hover-label (observation 5) and the awards-ceremony screen (observation 7).

original:behavior.summary: Assembled documented-behavior evidence for The Movies (2005) UI from the official Lionhead/Activision game manual (primary source, read in full + 8 rendered pages viewed as images), a GameFAQs walkthrough (v3.0), PCGamingWiki, and three Fandom wiki facility pages (all retrieved via Wayback Machine after live sites blocked WebFetch/curl with Cloudflare challenges or 403/402). Covers: HUD frame/layout, Star Cards and Movie Card icon-by-stage system, Information Bubbles (hover/right-click/priority-sort/threshold bars), Pips, universal click/drag/delete interaction grammar, room-based drag-and-drop hiring/casting for every facility, the Guiding Streams hint system, pause/play/fast-forward semantics, Cash Balance dual-entry navigation, the lot-attractiveness heatmap overlay, a three-channel mood-alert escalation ladder, Custom Scriptwriting Office's per-scene shot-tracking, Script Office tier gating, and documented widescreen/HUD-scaling failures on modern displays. Each observation includes a design lesson and explicit transfers/does-not-transfer calls for a modern isometric studio-management HUD. Casting Office's own Fandom page and any Molyneux/Edge/Eurogamer developer-commentary source could not be obtained this pass (flagged in unverified, not asserted as absent).
