observations.situation: Default in-game HUD, base game
observations.observation: Manual's labeled diagram shows the entire screen framed by a curved theater-marquee/poster border with a star-ribbon logo top-center; named zones are Timeline (top, full width), Date/Pause/Play/FF (top-left), Cash Balance & Studio Ranking (top-right), Star Cards (left edge, stacked), Movie Cards (right edge, stacked), Build Button (bottom-left).
observations.designLesson: The ornamental frame itself does brand/setting work, not just the icons inside it.
observations.transfers: A themed ornamental frame reinforcing setting (soundstage/clapperboard motif) rather than a neutral flat-UI bar.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The literal fixed-pixel frame is exactly what fails at non-4:3 resolutions (see resolution-scaling observation).

observations.situation: Star Cards on left HUD edge
observations.observation: "Star Cards — these images represent the Stars... By using the buttons above the Star cards, you can cycle through your studio's other employees." Only one card shown at a time with prev/next arrows; left-click jumps camera to them, hold-left-click-drag relocates them, right-click shows all info bubbles instantly.
observations.designLesson: Single-card-plus-cycle-arrows deliberately narrows attention to one person rather than a scannable roster.
observations.transfers: Card-as-draggable-object (grab a portrait, drop it onto the world to reassign) is a strong interaction to reuse.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Serial one-card cycling does not scale past a small roster; needs a searchable/filterable grid fallback in a modern build.

observations.situation: Right-edge Movie Cards
observations.observation: Six distinct icon states shown and captioned verbatim: script/quill ("scriptwriters busily working"), script+checkmark ("ready for casting"), third icon ("ready to shoot"), movie-camera ("in the process of being filmed"), film-can ("shot and ready for release"), film-can-with-graphic ("released... a $ sign will pulse over the movie card" while earning). Genre glyphs (fist/glasses/skull/lips/alien head) in upper-right corner.
observations.designLesson: Stage-of-production is communicated purely via icon substitution on a persistent card; the only animated cue (pulsing $) is reserved for active revenue.
observations.transfers: Icon-substitution-as-primary-stage-indicator, and reserving animation for the one truly time/money-sensitive state.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The manual's low-contrast icon rendering; some stage icons (script vs script+check) are too subtly differentiated for a modern colorblind-safe HUD.

observations.situation: Hovering or right-clicking any Star/movie/building/card
observations.observation: Bubbles appear on hover after a wait (duration unspecified); right-click shows all info instantly; bubbles are priority-sorted ("intelligently work out which information is of the highest priority and display this first"); red '!' = urgent, blue 'i' = informational; click a bubble to "burst" it, click the central bubble to close the whole group; bars have visible mood "thresholds" with real mechanical consequences below/above them.
observations.designLesson: Priority-sorting plus a group-dismiss gesture makes an otherwise noisy tooltip system self-limiting.
observations.transfers: Priority-sorted, glyph-coded (not color-only) hover urgency; group-dismiss gesture; threshold bars tied to real consequences.
observations.doesNotTransfer: World-space floating bubble clusters anchored to moving figures would clutter a busier modern scene; centralize into a docked panel instead.

observations.situation: Hover-triggered information bubbles
observations.observation: Small screenshot shows 4-5 oval bubble panels connected by thin lines radiating from one walking character on the lot, confirming bubbles are diegetic world-anchored call-outs.
observations.designLesson: Bubbles are rendered as physically-anchored call-outs, not a fixed side panel.
observations.transfers: n/a (see paired documented-behavior observation).
observations.doesNotTransfer: n/a

observations.situation: Ambient studio-wide status changes
observations.observation: "Pips" are a second, separate alert layer: small icons that appear and fade as studio status changes, red background = negative, green background = positive; distinct from on-demand information bubbles.
observations.designLesson: Two parallel notification tiers: rich on-demand bubbles vs. terse unprompted pips — a toast-vs-inspector split.
observations.transfers: The two-tier ambient-toast + on-demand-detail split.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Reliance on red/green fill alone for polarity is a colorblind-accessibility risk; shape variation visible in the art is not confirmed sufficient.

observations.situation: Interacting with people/HUD icons/ornaments/facilities
observations.observation: Table: Person left-click=Pick Up/Drop, right-click=info; Star/Movie HUD icon left-click=Select to Move/Drop, right-click=info; Lot Ornaments left-click=Duplicate into hand, right-click=See Move Options; Facilities left-click=Show Floorplan.
observations.designLesson: A small, consistent click/right-click grammar covers nearly every object type in the game.
observations.transfers: A consistent, small interaction grammar reused across every draggable object type.
observations.doesNotTransfer: n/a

observations.situation: Deleting a building vs. deleting an ornament
observations.observation: Buildings: "hold a building over the bomb and wait for the small squares around it to fill. Let go... and you will be left with a load of rubbish to clean up." Ornaments/plants: hover to highlight, left-click-hold to grab, then right-click to delete (right-click overloaded to mean 'destroy held item' vs. 'inspect' when empty-handed).
observations.designLesson: The same right-click button is overloaded by held-item state, and destructive building removal carries extra hold-to-confirm friction that cheap ornament removal does not.
observations.transfers: State-dependent button overloading and confirmation friction scaled to the cost of the mistake.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The literal 'bomb' icon metaphor reads ambiguously (sabotage vs. demolish) out of context; keep the hold-to-fill affordance with a clearer glyph.

observations.situation: Hiring builders/writers/actors/casting a movie
observations.observation: Every hiring/assignment action is: pick a person up (left-click-hold) -> drag across the 3D world -> drop into a labeled sub-room of a building (Create Builder room, hire actor/director rooms, genre script rooms, Begin Casting room, Shoot It room, PR room, Reviews room, Finance room, Makeover/Nip&Tuck/Liposuction/Implants rooms). Casting Office specifically: left-click the building to 'lower the walls' and reveal an interior floorplan of droppable rooms.
observations.designLesson: There is no menu-based hiring UI at all; every assignment is spatial and building-scoped.
observations.transfers: Spatial, room-based assignment as a legible 'this job belongs to this building' metaphor for headline actions.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Pure drag-and-drop for every action does not scale to hundreds of staff; needs a searchable/filterable list fallback the original apparently lacked.

observations.situation: Returning to the Casting Office mid-shoot to recast
observations.observation: "putting actors into different roles or getting a new director will make your movie start shooting from the start. This does not happen when changing crew or extras." No proactive warning dialog is described.
observations.designLesson: An important, costly rule (recasting a lead resets the whole shoot) is enforced silently as a drop consequence rather than surfaced via a confirmation dialog.
observations.transfers: The recast-lead-resets vs. recast-crew-doesn't asymmetry as a design rule.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Enforcing it with zero warning to the player is a usability gap worth fixing (add an explicit confirmation) rather than reproducing.

observations.situation: Picking up any Star, movie, script, or queued person
observations.observation: "you'll see a trail of stars leading you to perform the most sensible action. This is only a suggestion... These also display on the Build menu." Tab key = 'Go to the end of highest priority sparkling stream.'
observations.designLesson: One lightweight, dismissible, world-space+menu-space hint system replaces separate 3D and UI tutorials.
observations.transfers: A single ignorable suggested-next-step affordance spanning both the 3D world and 2D menus.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The literal sparkling-star VFX is period/brand flavor, not the mechanic itself.

observations.situation: Pausing the game
observations.observation: "When you pause the game, you can still perform many tasks and check the status... You won't be able to pick up and drop items in the studio such as Stars, staff, movies or scripts when time is paused." A dedicated pause icon beneath the timeline toggles pause without the full Esc menu; P is a direct keyboard toggle.
observations.designLesson: Pause is explicitly 'audit yes, manipulate no,' keeping world-state edits tied to flowing time.
observations.transfers: Clearly documenting/communicating exactly what pause does and does not allow.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Blanket-blocking all drag-drop during pause would frustrate players used to modern pause-and-plan sims; should be a deliberate choice, not silent inheritance.

observations.situation: Checking/adjusting Star salaries
observations.observation: Two independent routes to the same Salary screen: (1) click Cash Balance in HUD -> click arrow on Finance screen edge; (2) drag a Star (or the floating 'I' info icon) into the Finance room of the Production Office, per GameFAQs (S2).
observations.designLesson: Critical numeric state gets both a fast click-through path and a diegetic drag-into-room path to the same destination.
observations.transfers: Dual on-ramps (fast direct + diegetic physical) to the same deep screen.
observations.doesNotTransfer: n/a

observations.situation: Studio going into debt
observations.observation: "Your balance can go into the red but when you're in debt, you won't be able to build new sets or add certain facilities and lot ornamentation." No on-screen HUD warning is described for this state anywhere in the manual.
observations.designLesson: A real mechanical penalty exists but is documented only in the manual, not surfaced live in the HUD.
observations.transfers: n/a — this is a gap to fix, not a pattern to copy.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Silent debt penalties with no HUD cue should not be repeated; recolor the cash figure or add a persistent pip instead.

observations.situation: Checking overall lot appeal (key L)
observations.observation: "You'll see shades of green and red in the area by the buildings you have constructed so far. The greener an area appears, the more attractive it is... you'll see the level of redness fade and eventually turn green as you add further flora."
observations.designLesson: Aggregate spatial stats are shown as a toggleable full-ground heatmap overlay, not a checklist or icon badges, with live-updating feedback as you build.
observations.transfers: A toggleable full-lot heatmap overlay bound to one key for an aggregate spatial stat (directly analogous to modern city-builders' land-value/pollution overlays).
observations.doesNotTransfer: Nothing — this is one of the cleanest, most directly reusable ideas found.

observations.situation: Star mood/relationship state across three channels
observations.observation: World-space: "thought bubbles that appear when two Stars are interacting" / GameFAQs: "speech bubbles that appear above their heads." HUD: GameFAQs describes an award-unlocked 'green bars flashing' cue on the salary/mood bar. Audio: "listen for announcements over the studio PA system that help keep you up to date with problems."
observations.designLesson: The same underlying state is exposed via three escalating channels: ambient world cue, HUD status cue, and an audio interrupt that reaches the player regardless of camera position.
observations.transfers: The ambient-to-HUD-to-audio escalation ladder concept, reserved for genuinely important events.
observations.doesNotTransfer: A bare color-only flash (green flashing bar) with no shape/icon differentiation repeats a colorblind-accessibility gap.

observations.situation: Re-editing/re-shooting a movie in the Custom Scriptwriting Office
observations.observation: "If you drop a completed movie into this, any scene that is already shot will have a small green checkmark on it. Once you exit the making screen and essentially re-cast and re-shoot the movie, the game will be smart enough to skip any scenes with that green check mark."
observations.designLesson: Per-scene shot-status is tracked and shown inside the advanced editor, nested one level finer than the whole-movie-card icon shown in the main HUD.
observations.transfers: Nesting a fine-grained per-unit status indicator inside a detailed editor beneath a coarse whole-object HUD indicator (comparable to per-shot render status in a modern pipeline tool).
observations.doesNotTransfer: n/a

observations.situation: Script Office progression
observations.observation: Four priced tiers (Basic $6,000/1-star cap, Intermediate $29,000/2-star, Proficient $33,333/3-star, First Class $66,666/4-star); GameFAQs corroborates that Proficient and First Class "have to be unlocked by winning awards," and the manual/GameFAQs corroborate the cap also governs the Custom Scriptwriting Office's max output.
observations.designLesson: Progression is a visible, ownable building upgrade with a hard numeric ceiling, not an abstract tech tree, and one upgrade raises the ceiling for two different production paths.
observations.transfers: Tying an abstract quality cap to a single visible building tier rather than a hidden meta-currency.
observations.doesNotTransfer: n/a

observations.situation: Running the game at non-native/ultrawide resolutions today
observations.observation: "Models and HUD are stretched to fit the screen, and some menu items have distorted text" (Ultra-widescreen row); "Menus and some UI elements are locked to 30 FPS" (60 FPS row); Widescreen resolution flagged as needing an external WSGF workaround, i.e., not natively clean.
observations.designLesson: A HUD authored for one fixed reference aspect ratio breaks visually (stretching, distorted text) when force-scaled to modern displays, and some UI logic is separately frame-rate-locked.
observations.transfers: n/a (cautionary).
observations.doesNotTransfer: The rigid, single-resolution-assumption HUD architecture itself must not be repeated; build layout and hit-testing from one responsive system so aspect-ratio changes can't desync visuals from click targets.

observations.situation: Community 'Fixer' patch for The Movies
observations.observation: WebSearch snippet describes the fixer as unlocking the resolution selector, correcting FOV/2D-interface aspect ratio, and 'fixes button click areas to match the corrected interface dimensions' — implying stock click-hitboxes desync from the visuals once resolution changes.
observations.designLesson: If accurate, this is a second, more severe failure mode beyond visual stretching: functional misalignment between what's drawn and what's clickable.
observations.transfers: n/a (cautionary lead, not independently confirmed).
observations.doesNotTransfer: n/a

workflowsTraced.name: Make and release one movie, start to finish

steps.whatHappens: Hire builders: left-click a person in the Staff Office queue, drag, drop into the 'Create Builder' room (hovering the correct sub-area highlights it blue).
Click Build icon (bottom-left) -> Facilities -> Stage School -> position the flat building outline (yellow = buildable, red = obstructed) -> builders auto-construct it.
A queue of walk-in hopefuls forms outside the Stage School; drag-drop them into Actor/Director/Extra rooms to hire.
Build a Script Office; drag a scriptwriter into the room matching the desired genre; drag additional writers into the shared script pool to speed writing.
Build a Casting Office; left-click the building itself to 'lower the walls' and reveal its interior floorplan of role rooms.
Drag the movie/script icon from the HUD's right-edge Movie Card rail into the 'Begin Casting' room, then drop actors/directors/extras/crew into their respective rooms.
Drag the movie icon into the 'Shoot It' room to begin filming; filming happens on a placed Set (a required set shown in red in the info bubble means it's missing/busy/damaged).

Drag the completed movie into the Production Office's 'Release' room (optionally drag it onto a marketing-budget amount first if a Publicity Office exists); dragging into 'Movie Player' instead previews it uncut.
Release automatically triggers the Review screen showing critics' comments before returning control to the player.

observations.situation: Main studio-lot view, mid-game (13 Jul 1937 timestamp), isometric painterly lot with buildings, weather/lighting overlays, NPC dots
observations.observation: The lot is the permanent home screen: top bar holds date/speed controls + 4 resource counters (cash, budget, 'insight'/eye icon, 'star' currency); left side shows a scrollable objectives list; right-center floating cards stack up to 3 in-progress scripts with writer name, star rating, and dual percentage bars (approval/dislike style meters) directly on the lot, no modal needed; bottom-right shows a row of 4 finished-film cards with revenue and two quality-score numbers (film icon + comedy-mask icon) plus a status ribbon (READY / alert-red 'X D.' countdown); a bottom hex-node timeline strip runs the full width showing project pipeline stages as connected icons.
observations.designLesson: Persistent, glanceable studio state (in-flight scripts + finished films + objectives) lives ON the lot canvas as floating cards rather than behind a menu click — the world never disappears while checking status.
observations.transfers: A left people-rail + right pictures-rail HUD should keep the equivalent 'projects in flight' and 'finished/ready' cards visible as compact docked panels over the lot, not gated behind a separate screen, so status is ambient.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The sheer number of stacked floating cards + a bottom hex-timeline + top resource bar + left objectives list simultaneously is a lot of concurrent HUD chrome for a 2D isometric screen at phone/laptop scale — should be reduced/collapsed rather than copied wholesale.

observations.situation: Full-screen 'Pollux 1933' awards ceremony cutscene screen
observations.observation: A dedicated full-screen non-lot scene (Art Deco theater interior, painted static background) replaces the world entirely for awards; three nominee cards along the bottom show portrait, name, and film title with a small badge (studio insignia) per nominee; a single 'Pause' control is the only interactive element besides presumably 'next'.
observations.designLesson: High-ceremony, low-frequency events (awards) get a full-screen theatrical treatment that deliberately breaks continuity — used sparingly, this is a legitimate way to mark a special beat as distinct from routine management.
observations.transfers: An annual awards/milestone event can justify a full-screen take-over in the target HUD, since it is rare and meant to feel like a reward, not routine navigation.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Per Game8/GameLuster reviews, transitions like this 'cannot be skipped or turned off' and become 'a chore' with multiple concurrent projects — any full-screen takeover in the new HUD must be skippable/toggleable from the first build.

observations.situation: 'New Scandal' decision popup over a dimmed/grayscale lot background
observations.observation: Portrait card (illustrated headshot, name, role icon, star rating, two numeric meters with an info-i) sits beside a full-width illustrated scene image (police officer writing up a shoplifting actress) and a plain-language incident description, ending in a single 'Continue' button. The background lot desaturates to gray to push all focus onto the modal.
observations.designLesson: Contextual full-attention decision popups pair a portrait+stat card with a narrative illustration and short text, then a single low-friction acknowledgement button when no real choice exists (informational events) versus the multi-choice format used for real decisions (see Select an Operation, ss_11).
observations.transfers: For narrative/incident beats (a star scandal, a staff issue) a portrait-card + short illustrated vignette + one dismiss button is a clean, readable pattern for a 2D HUD's alert layer.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The desaturate-whole-world treatment is heavy-handed for frequent, low-stakes events; reserve full desaturation for genuinely serious alerts, not routine flavor text, to avoid the 'clicking through many menus/interrupts' fatigue Steam forum threads report.

observations.situation: Distribution/scheduling screen for the film 'Esprit de Corps', full-screen (not lot-contextual)
observations.observation: Left 2/3 is a horizontal Gantt-style calendar (weeks across top) showing the player's film as a green block among competitor films (dark blocks with studio-initial badges) on parallel rows, so competitive scheduling collisions are visually obvious; a hover tooltip shows exact screenings/price; right 1/3 breaks out a 'Weekly Screening Schedule' table (4 rows, 'Our' vs 'Other' sliders with numeric counts) and a 'Film Copies Printing' vendor card with per-copy price and turnaround time.
observations.designLesson: A genuinely complex negotiation (distribution slots, print costs, competing releases) is given its own full-screen dedicated view with a timeline metaphor — this is the right call for a decision this data-dense; it should NOT be jammed into a lot-side panel.
observations.transfers: Complex, infrequent, numbers-heavy negotiations (e.g., distribution deals, financing) belong in a dedicated full-screen view with a timeline/calendar visualization, reserving the lot+rails HUD for frequent, lightweight glances.
observations.doesNotTransfer: GameLuster's review explicitly flags this exact screen as a UX failure: 'the optimum number of those rentals is never well defined... you're either overbooking... or underbooking' — the raw slider/number density here is the failure mode, not the model; the target HUD should compute or recommend an optimum rather than exposing all raw sliders.

observations.situation: Reviewer describing distribution booking and staff-role legibility
observations.observation: Quoted: "the optimum number of those rentals is never well defined. Which means that you're either overbooking (and losing money) or underbooking (and losing money)" and staff role/genre preference clarity 'the demo gave you the straight dope on preferred roles and genres' but the shipped build obscures this for pre-existing staff, feeling 'dissonant' for veteran hires.
observations.designLesson: Reported frustration (dated: GameLuster EA review, published shortly after 10 Apr 2025 launch) is with information WITHHELD or requiring inference, not with density per se — players want the system to state constraints (ideal booking count) and staff preferences directly rather than making them guess from indirect signals.
observations.transfers: Whenever a compact card shows a stat, add a clear 'ideal/target' marker or preference tag directly on the card (e.g., preferred genre icon on a staff portrait) rather than requiring the player to infer it from history.
observations.doesNotTransfer: N/A — this is a pure content/legibility lesson, no visual pattern to avoid copying.

observations.situation: Film pre-production team-assembly screen for 'Esprit de Corps' (script buildout already locked, now casting)
observations.observation: Four large role cards (Producer, Director, Detective/Protagonist, Evil Witch/Antagonist) each show portrait, name, age, one decimal star rating, two colored progress bars (pink 'dislike'/orange or green 'like'-style meters with an eye/mask icon), and a row of small genre/role icons with a lock/lookup slot. A right-hand summary column totals cost+time as an equation (pre-production + filming = total $/days), plus a checklist of physical production choices (locations, filming tech, sound tech, extras count, costume tier, crew size) and the assigned scriptwriter's card repeated with the same rating language. A stepper at bottom (Locations > Technologies > Team > Confirmation) shows wizard progress.
observations.designLesson: A consistent 'talent card' language (portrait, star rating, two colored meters, small icon row for genre/role fit) is reused everywhere talent appears — casting, scripting, scandal, hiring — giving instant visual recognition of 'this is a person and here is their fit' regardless of context.
observations.transfers: Establish one canonical portrait-card component (portrait + 1 headline rating + 2 max secondary meters + small icon row) and reuse it verbatim across every screen that shows a person — the right pictures-rail and any casting/hiring modal — for cross-screen legibility.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The wizard-style multi-step (Locations→Technologies→Team→Confirmation) full-screen flow for assembling a single film is heavy process for what could be a fast decision; a compact studio HUD should let simple casting happen as a lighter overlay, reserving full wizards for genuinely first-time or complex setups.

observations.situation: Script-building 'Story Workshop' card-slotting screen for 'The Third Policeman'
observations.observation: Central 3x4 grid of face-up story-element cards already placed (Cop, Criminal Gang, Angry Boss, Brother in Arms, Rival, Captured & Tortured, etc., '9/10 filled'), each a small icon-illustrated tarot-like card with tiny gender-availability glyphs; top strip shows 3 genre sliders as percentage bars (Detective/Drama/Action) recomputed live as cards are chosen; right panel is a scrollable palette of selectable finale/element cards grouped by category tab icons at the top, with a hover tooltip expanding the selected card's flavor text ('Protagonist Dies Heroically...').
observations.designLesson: A tactile card-based 'deckbuilder' metaphor turns an abstract data-entry task (choosing plot beats) into a visually legible, game-like interaction: percentage genre bars react live to card choices, giving immediate feedback on tonal composition.
observations.transfers: For any 'compose a project from discrete story/creative elements' feature, a card-grid-plus-live-recompute-meter pattern communicates composition and consequence far better than dropdowns or checkboxes — worth adapting to a script/greenlight screen in the target HUD.
observations.doesNotTransfer: This is a genuinely full-screen, focused-attention minigame screen — it deliberately hides the lot and resource bar entirely (no top HUD visible in this shot); that total context-loss is appropriate only for a deliberate, occasional creative-focus task, not for anything that should stay contextual.

observations.situation: 'Secrets' full-screen dashboard listing blackmail/dark-secret risk cards
observations.observation: A responsive grid of colored severity-banner cards (pink 'MAXIMUM RISK', orange 'HIGH RISK', green 'MINIMUM RISK') each naming the secret ('Murdered Bessie Patterson'), a countdown to risk decrease, a small portrait+stats card for the informed NPC with a 3-segment color-coded probability bar (red/orange/green %), and an 'Agent on duty' timer or an 'Assign security' CTA slot.
observations.designLesson: Color-coded severity banners (pink/orange/green) at the top of otherwise-identical cards let a player triage a list of many similar items (8+ visible, more via scrollbar) at a glance without reading each one.
observations.transfers: A severity-color banner strip atop any alert/risk card is a fast, reusable way to make a long list scannable — directly applicable to a studio HUD's crisis/alert queue.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The specific dark content (murder/blackmail secrets) is thematic to this game's Prohibition-era noir tone and not a mechanic to imitate; only the visual triage pattern transfers.

observations.situation: 'Select an Operation' full-screen dark-side action-choice screen (surveillance/kidnapping menu)
observations.observation: Left column: single target portrait card with name/age/rating/two meters/genre+role icon rows (same canonical card as elsewhere) plus a 'Selected Operation' preview box and a 'Duration of Surveillance' empty field. Right: 2x2 grid of large illustrated operation choice tiles (Threat/Beating/Kidnapping/Killing), each a monochrome noir illustration with an icon+label+one-line consequence description; the selected tile gets a gold border highlight.
observations.designLesson: For real, mutually-exclusive multi-choice decisions (as opposed to the single-button acknowledgement in ss_03), the game switches to large illustrated tiles with a clear selected-state border, one line of consequence text per option, and separates 'who this affects' (left card) from 'what you're choosing' (right grid) — a clean decision-screen anatomy.
observations.transfers: The two-zone anatomy — persistent subject/target card on one side, mutually-exclusive illustrated choice tiles with selected-state highlight on the other — is a strong reusable template for any studio-HUD decision popup with several distinct options and consequences.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Nothing structurally to avoid; only the content (violent dark-side ops) is not relevant to a family-friendlier or more business-focused studio sim.

observations.situation: Reviewer general impression of the interface
observations.observation: Quoted: "The UI is still good and contextual. The building designs are period appropriate," alongside criticism that outcome feedback after a shoot is opaque ('too many elements point to bad times on set without breaking down exactly what happened').
observations.designLesson: Positive baseline: contextual UI + strong period art direction (Deco motifs, period-appropriate iconography, muted sepia/noir palette) is a real strength worth crediting, confirmed independently in the screenshots (gold Deco borders/hex frames throughout every screen, ss_01 through ss_11) — but the game is criticized for withholding causal explanation of WHY an outcome happened, only presenting the outcome number.
observations.transfers: Pair every outcome number/status change on cards or in reports with a short causal explanation (a 'why' line), not just a delta number — avoids the reported frustration of 'bad times on set' with no breakdown.
observations.doesNotTransfer: N/A

observations.situation: Aggregated Steam Community discussion feedback (WebSearch snippet, threads not individually opened)
observations.observation: Reported complaint (unverified individually, low confidence): navigation requires scrolling around the lot/screen to reach menus per-building and per-film; awkward zoom levels; important info like near-bankruptcy or lapsing staff contracts can be missed without deep menu-diving.
observations.designLesson: Reported frustration is about critical-state surfacing (contracts, bankruptcy risk) failing to interrupt/alert proactively, and camera/navigation friction from a large scrollable isometric map.
observations.transfers: Critical financial/staffing thresholds (about to run out of cash, contract expiring) should push a proactive top-of-screen alert badge rather than requiring the player to scroll/hunt on the lot to notice — directly informs the target HUD's 'critical alerts' requirement.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The literal large-freely-scrollable isometric lot with per-building menus is the source of the navigation complaint; a studio HUD with a fixed central lot + docked rails (rather than an open-world-style pannable map) avoids this failure mode by construction.

steps.whatHappens: Wizard stepper: Locations > Technologies > Team > Confirmation; Team step shows 4 role cards (Producer/Director/Protagonist/Antagonist) each with portrait+rating+like/dislike meters+genre icon row, plus a running cost+time equation and a physical-production checklist on the right.

steps.whatHappens: Grid of already-placed element cards (9/10 filled) with live-updating genre percentage bars at top; right-hand palette of selectable cards grouped by category tabs, tooltip shows flavor text on hover/select.

Target portrait card fixed on left; 2x2 illustrated tile grid of mutually exclusive severity options on right; selecting a tile gold-highlights it and populates a 'Selected Operation' preview box before a final 'Select an Agent' CTA.

comp:hollywoodanimal.summary: Hollywood Animal (Weappy Studio, Steam Early Access since 10 Apr 2025, Act 1 content scope, evidence gathered from 14 official Steam screenshots viewed directly plus two Early Access reviews) shows a mature, thematically coherent Art-Deco/noir visual language and a genuinely useful pattern worth transferring: one canonical 'talent card' (portrait + single headline star rating + up to 2 secondary meters + small icon row) reused identically across the lot, casting, scandal, and dark-ops screens, plus a clean two-zone decision-screen anatomy (fixed subject card + illustrated mutually-exclusive choice tiles) and severity-color-banner triage cards for alert lists. Its lot view keeps in-flight scripts and finished films visible as floating cards without leaving the world, which is the right instinct for a studio HUD's persistent awareness goal. Its clear failure modes, independently confirmed by two reviewers and Steam Community threads, are: un-skippable full-screen transitions that become tedious across multiple concurrent projects; a distribution/booking screen that exposes raw sliders and numbers without ever stating an 'ideal' target, forcing guesswork; outcome feedback that shows a result number without a causal 'why'; and a large freely-scrollable isometric map whose per-building menus and awkward zoom make critical alerts (bankruptcy risk, lapsing contracts) easy to miss. All of these transfer directly as concrete do/don't guidance for a 2D isometric studio HUD with a left people-rail, right pictures-rail, and central lot.
unverified: Exact current patch/build number beyond 'Early Access since 10 Apr 2025' — Weappy does not expose version numbers on the Steam store or screenshots; observations should be read as 'as of the Early Access build available ~Sep 2026', not tied to a specific patch.

Whether the specific UI complaints found via WebSearch snippet (scrolling/zoom navigation, missed bankruptcy/contract alerts) come from reviews dated at launch (Apr 2025) or later in Early Access — the individual Steam Community thread pages were not opened directly, only an aggregated search snippet was read, so this is marked LOW confidence and sourced as documented-behavior at one remove.
No developer UI/art blog post or postmortem was found in this search pass; observations rely on screenshots + player-facing reviews only, not developer commentary on design intent.

observations.situation: Build/room-placement mode, general play
observations.observation: Two independently-anchored corner clusters: a vertical stack of 4 rounded-square icon buttons pinned bottom-left (build/manage tools), and a separate dark-teal capsule pinned bottom-right holding cash, reputation dial, play/pause/fast-forward transport, and in-game date. They are never merged into one continuous bottom bar.
observations.designLesson: Separating glanceable passive status (cash/time/speed) from active action tools (build/hire) into two small distinct corner clusters, rather than one long bar, keeps each cluster small and fast to read.
observations.transfers: A left people-rail/right pictures-rail HUD can similarly keep transport+resource status in one small anchored cluster and build/action tools in another, rather than fusing everything into a single strip.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The specific corner assignment (build bottom-left, money bottom-right) is arbitrary to this game's control scheme, not a positional rule to copy.

observations.situation: Placing an Office Desk in a GP's Office build screen
observations.observation: A slim left-edge vertical list shows 6-8 rows, each one icon + item name + price (Door $75, Window $60, Filing Cabinet $100, Office Desk $250, Examination Table $250, Bookcase $200, Plant $90, Bin $50); the row for the item currently being placed (Office Desk) is highlighted solid yellow against an otherwise flat teal field. A top bar spanning most of the screen width shows the room name ("GP's Office") and current action ("Place Office Desk"), plus a prestige-star counter and level indicator.
observations.designLesson: A single unmistakable saturated highlight color (yellow on teal) marks the 'currently armed' selection; the top contextual bar narrates what the side list is doing so the two panels read as one instrument rather than disconnected widgets.
observations.transfers: Using one strong, consistent highlight color for 'currently selected/armed' state, and linking a top strip to narrate whichever rail (people or pictures) is currently active, reduces the amount of UI state a viewer must hold in their head.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The list itself is very sparse — one icon and one price per row, no secondary stats — which matches Theme Hospital-era simplicity but would look under-detailed for a management HUD needing 2-3 stat readouts per row (e.g., staff skill + mood + wage).

observations.situation: Sampled across ~40 frames spanning build mode, placement mode, and an in-progress complaint alert
observations.observation: The isometric hospital view is never covered by more than the left rail plus top/bottom bars (roughly the outer ~15% of the frame) in any sampled frame; even an active complaint alert renders as a small ticker, not a modal.
observations.designLesson: Management UI is a permanent frame around a living diorama, never a takeover screen — consistent with the developer's stated intent to keep the UI 'accessible' rather than intimidating (see S4 quotes).
observations.transfers: Keeping the central lot always visible behind every panel (build, alerts, info) reinforces a living-space feel rather than a series of menus — directly supports never replacing the central lot with a full-screen sub-app in a people-rail/pictures-rail HUD.

observations.situation: Developer retrospective interview
observations.observation: Design director Gary Carr, quoted: "A lot of PC games have very small icons which look incredibly complex. The original Theme Hospital had chunky and accessible UI that didn't intimidate people." And: "Make people think it's easy to use and then further down it gets more complex. If people don't want to dig deeper they can still play." Producer Mark Webley: "We probably underestimated just how much work the UI was going to be."
observations.designLesson: The studio deliberately designed a shallow, large-icon first layer (confirmed visually in the sparse 6-8 row build list) with deeper systems (staff traits, diagnosis chains) held behind further clicks, so a first screen never looks statistically dense.
observations.transfers: A progressive-disclosure philosophy — keep default always-visible chrome large-icon and low-count, push secondary detail (traits, multi-stat comparisons) into a click-through inspector — directly informs how much should live on always-visible people/pictures rails versus behind a click.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The specific 'claymation-looking,' chunky-icon aesthetic is a stylistic choice tied to Two Point's comedic tone; it should inform density/hierarchy decisions, not dictate that a different game's rails must adopt the same toylike icon rendering.

observations.situation: Official Steam screenshots vs. S2 UI frames, compared side by side
observations.observation: The flat teal used for the left item-list panel and top status bar (O2) closely matches the mint/teal flooring and pale blue-grey wall trim used throughout the hospital corridors in steam_ss_5.jpg and steam_ss_7.jpg; the world's rounded-corner, flat-shaded 'clean plastic/toy' material language is echoed by the UI's own rounded-rect icon buttons and flat teal fields.
observations.designLesson: Sampling the UI chrome hue directly from the dominant environment palette (not a generic dark or white app chrome) makes the interface read as part of the same object as the world.
observations.transfers: Sampling 1-2 of the lot's own dominant environment colors for persistent rail backgrounds is a cheap way to make a 2D isometric studio HUD feel unified with its world.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The exact hue (mint/teal) carries a 'clean, clinical' connotation specific to a hospital; a film-studio lot would want its own sampled palette (sun-bleached concrete, soundstage grey, marquee gold) rather than literally reusing hospital teal.

observations.situation: A patient complaint firing mid-session in the pre-release build
observations.observation: The alert text "A patient has had enough of the way you are running the hospital and has stormed out!" renders as a single-line dark ticker roughly 1/6 of screen width, anchored just above the bottom-left build cluster; gameplay and camera continue uninterrupted, with a small 'ghost' figure in the world indicating the departed patient.
observations.designLesson: Even a fairly serious failure signal (lost patient/reputation) is communicated via a transient, corner-anchored text strip rather than a screen-pausing dialog.
observations.transfers: Routing 'needs attention' alerts (a stalled project, an unhappy crew member) through a small persistent ticker near an existing rail, instead of a popup dialog, keeps the player in flow — consistent with a non-modal management HUD.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Only one alert severity (a minor complaint) was observed in this pre-release build; there is no evidence here about whether more severe events (e.g., an outbreak) escalate to a modal in the shipped 1.0+ game — do not generalize this to all alert severities.

comp:twopoint.summary: Studied Two Point Hospital's management UI via official primary sources only: 10 official Steam screenshots (viewed 5), a developer-commentary gameplay video from the official Two Point Studios channel (pre-1.0 'Coming 2018' build — extracted and viewed a contact sheet plus 5 full-resolution frames, then deleted the video), the official 60-second launch trailer (contact sheet, then deleted), and a developer-interview retrospective (MCV/DEVELOP) with direct Gary Carr / Mark Webley quotes on UI philosophy. Two fan UI-teardown sites and the Fandom Staff wiki page returned HTTP 403/Cloudflare blocks and could not be read directly, so the staff-portrait/trait-card 'meaningful compact status' angle from the brief is NOT independently confirmed in this pass (flagged O8/unverified) — this is the one notable gap. Confirmed observations (all from the pre-release developer-commentary video, cross-checked against Steam screenshots for palette): two small independently-anchored bottom-corner clusters split passive status (cash/time/speed) from active tools (build/hire) rather than one continuous bar; a single strong saturated highlight color (yellow-on-teal) marks the currently-armed build selection, tied to a top contextual bar that narrates the active room/action; the isometric lot is never obscured by more than ~15% of the frame by any panel, including alerts, which render as small non-modal corner tickers; and the UI chrome hue is sampled directly from the game's own dominant environment palette rather than generic app chrome, reinforcing world/UI material coherence. Developer quotes corroborate a deliberate 'chunky, non-intimidating, shallow-first-layer' philosophy with complexity held behind further clicks. Official marketing screenshots and the launch trailer were confirmed to contain zero HUD chrome, which is itself a useful methodological finding: such assets are art-direction evidence only, never UI evidence.

comp:anno.summary: Studied Anno 1800's base-game management UI via the official Anno Union dev blog (UI design philosophy + visual feedback systems), official Steam marketing screenshots, a downloaded 480p no-commentary gameplay walkthrough (12 frames extracted, video deleted after), and dated Steam Community threads on UI scaling. No official PDF manual exists from Ubisoft (only unverifiable third-party Scribd copies), so the dev blog substitutes as primary developer-voice evidence. Found: a thin persistent top HUD bar; contextual right-side info panels (not full-screen) for buildings/citizens; an in-world radial quick-build wheel (not a bottom drawer) for placement confirmation; a portrait-based citizen "Needs" card for workforce status; a single-at-a-time advisor-portrait toast for warnings (no confirmed multi-item notification stack in this session); a full-screen tabbed Statistics window reserved for cross-island/financial data; deliberately restrained (non-ornate) UI chrome despite an ornate 3D world, per direct designer quote; and a persistent, multi-year (2019-2023+) community complaint about missing real UI/font scaling, corroborated by fan-made scaling mods.

observations.situation: Continuous ~35 min vanilla gameplay session, tutorial island, camera panned freely across ocean/land/city views
observations.observation: A single thin, dark, semi-transparent top bar persists in every frame: treasury/population/influence numbers left, a resource-icon strip center-right, and the player's portrait avatar with a small notification badge (a '4' badge seen) top-right. The 3D world beneath is always fully visible and interactable; the bar never expands to occlude the lot.
observations.designLesson: A persistent status rail earns permanence by staying thin (~5% of vertical height) and low-saturation so it recedes while the world underneath stays fully legible and clickable at all times.
observations.transfers: A slim always-visible top strip (funds/reputation/critical counts + a badge on a team/avatar icon) for a 2D lot HUD, never a modal dashboard covering the lot.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The strip is icon+number only, no names — a people-management HUD needs name/role glanceability, which belongs in a dedicated left rail, not copied into the top strip's density.

observations.situation: Selecting a building-under-construction, a placed production building, and a citizen's home at four different points in the session (960s, 1140s, 1470s, 1620s)
observations.observation: Each selection slides in a right-edge parchment-brown beveled panel (~22% of screen width) with an icon/portrait header and 2-4 stat rows (construction cost, maintenance, or a citizen 'Needs' tab with a satisfaction bar). The 3D lot stays visible and pannable to the left; nothing dims or blocks input elsewhere.
observations.designLesson: Contextual side-panels sized to roughly a quarter of the screen keep the player in spatial mode (world still visible/pannable) rather than menu mode; reserve true full-screen treatment for genuinely cross-cutting data.
observations.transfers: A right pictures/detail rail that swaps content by selection instead of opening a new screen — proven at scale in a genre neighbor.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Anno's panel is single-purpose per selection (one building = one panel); it offers no evidence on how to handle multiple simultaneous contexts (a person AND a picture AND a lot event) needing to be shown at once — that gap must be solved independently.

observations.situation: Placing a building foundation (Lumberjack's Hut, then Sawmill) at two separate points in the session
observations.observation: After placing a foundation, a circular ring UI (2-6 pie-slice icon buttons, e.g. hammer/blueprint icons) appears centered on the foundation itself in world-space, with a label ribbon above naming the building, cost, and a countdown timer. This in-world radial is distinct from the separate bottom nav bar tabs ('Ship Menu / Tools / Construction / Management') that hold the actual build-category drawer.
observations.designLesson: Anchoring a small, context-specific action menu at the object's world position (not a fixed screen location) keeps the player's eyes near the point of interest, reducing HUD/lot eye-cycling.
observations.transfers: An in-world radial/pie action menu for on-lot objects (e.g. right-click a set piece for 'rush / staff / cancel') is a compact alternative to opening a full side panel for 2-4 option decisions.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The wheel is icon-only with no default text label, relying on a tooltip ribbon to disambiguate, trading discoverability for compactness — a HUD for less genre-fluent players should keep short text labels visible by default rather than copy pure icon-only wheel slices.

observations.situation: Clicking a resident's home to open its info card
observations.observation: The card is headed 'Content Farmer' with a painted portrait bust in warm sepia lighting, a tabbed body ('Needs' selected in blue vs. a shield-icon tab), a '1/10' person-count row, a green satisfaction bar with a shield glyph, an 'Incidents' footer with a coin figure and a wrench-cost figure, and a bottom-right 'Jump To Object' button.
observations.designLesson: Giving population status a named mood/state label plus one portrait plus one meter communicates workforce health faster than a numeric table; the portrait creates an emotional anchor that community feedback explicitly asked Blue Byte to lean into further.
observations.transfers: A left people rail built around portrait + one-line status/mood + a single meter per person is close to ideal density for 'who needs attention.'
observations.doesNotTransfer: The card is single-selection only (one household at a time) — there is no evidence Anno solved cross-roster triage (an aggregate 'everyone with unmet needs' list); a people rail showing many portraits at once must solve that separately.

observations.situation: A construction-material warning appearing while the player worked on connecting a Sawmill to storage, captured 60 seconds apart
observations.observation: A wide beige banner reading 'Timber needs to be stored in either a Trading Post or a Warehouse...' appears bottom-center with a small circular advisor-portrait on its left edge, sitting just above the permanent bottom nav bar, and persists unchanged across the two sampled frames while the underlying problem remains unresolved.
observations.designLesson: Routing 'you have a problem right now' messages through an advisor-portrait toast near the bottom (close to the build/action controls already in use) keeps the alert associated with an actor and near the fix, rather than an abstract badge in a far corner.
observations.transfers: A bottom or near-action alert with a small advisor/narrator face humanizes a warning and reads faster than a generic icon; a good model for e.g. 'this picture is blocked' or 'this set needs power.'
observations.doesNotTransfer: Only one warning was seen occupying this slot at a time in this session; no multi-item notification STACK was observed, and per Steam Community feedback (S5-adjacent reports) even the single-item version reportedly has dismiss-timing bugs — the brief's expectation of a proven notification stack is not evidenced here and should not be assumed solved by Anno's example.

observations.situation: A Statistics window opened once during the session, showing production/storage/finance/population-style tabs and a two-pane goods list + detail body scoped to the island 'Ditchwater'
observations.observation: Unlike the contextual side panels, this window occupies a large centered rectangle and dims the 3D world behind it; tab labels were only partially legible at the captured resolution.
observations.designLesson: Reserving true full-screen/modal treatment for genuinely cross-island or historical/chart data (not for anything with a clear single-object owner) is a sound split; single-object info stays contextual, aggregate/historical info goes modal.
observations.transfers: A full-screen 'Studio Ledger/Trends' view is appropriate for cross-lot financials or season-over-season charts; keep it rare and reachable only via a distinct, deliberate action, matching Anno's separation.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The specific tab taxonomy (Production/Storage/Finance/Population) is specific to Anno's trade simulation and was captured at low fidelity — treat it as a structural pattern only, not a literal template.

observations.situation: UI designer Khajag Jabaghchourian describing the team's UI design philosophy pre-release
observations.observation: Direct quote: the team prioritized 'form follows function' and functional design over artistic ornamentation, using darker/desaturated tones for the persistent HUD and reserving brighter colors for pop-up notifications. This is corroborated visually: captured panels are plain beveled dark-brown/parchment rectangles with a thin gold rule line, no scrollwork or filigree, while all period ornamentation (domed palaces, gilded roofs, lighthouses) lives in the 3D world content itself per S3 marketing screenshots.
observations.locator: S1 devblog text; corroborating frames at 960s/1140s into S4 and Steam screenshot IDs 9 and 16
observations.designLesson: This directly contradicts a naive assumption that 'era-themed chrome' means ornate borders on every panel — Anno's actual solution puts period flavor into the 3D content and portrait illustration style, keeping chrome itself nearly flat so text/icons stay legible at small sizes.
observations.transfers: Put studio-era personality into the lot art and portrait/card illustration style, not into heavy widget borders; keep panel chrome close to flat/neutral, using a light accent color and a period-adjacent display font only for titles.
observations.doesNotTransfer: This is not license to go fully flat/generic — Anno still uses a warm sepia/gold accent and a period-appropriate serif-adjacent title font to hint at setting without structural ornament; a studio HUD should follow that same light-touch accent approach rather than either extreme.

observations.situation: Steam Community support thread on font/UI size, spanning multiple dated posts
observations.observation: SirVanzeek (8 Mar 2023): 'I almost need a microscope to read the words on anything. Standard 1920 resolution fullscreen.' Official reply, Ubi_TheBerry (14 Mar 2023): 'You can enable Large Subtitles, but other text font can't be adjusted I'm afraid.' supershanks (23 Jun 2023) reported requesting a refund on a 4K monitor over the same issue. Corroborated by fan-made mods explicitly titled 'Smaller UI for Anno 1800' and 'UI Scale 70 percent' (S6).
observations.locator: Steam discussion thread dated Mar-Jun 2023; mod.io/Nexus mod listings undated
observations.designLesson: A rich, small-font, information-dense contextual-panel system (as in Observations 2 and 4) has a real cost at high-DPI/4K if font/UI scale is not a first-class settings option; this is a multi-year unresolved gap between shipped panel density and shipped scaling support.
observations.transfers: Ship an explicit UI-scale slider (not just a subtitle toggle) from day one if adopting Anno's dense-card approach — treat it as required infrastructure, not a later nice-to-have.
observations.doesNotTransfer: This is a warning about Anno's execution gap, not a UI-language lesson — don't copy the absence of scaling options; the underlying panel/card design is otherwise sound and separable from this flaw.

observations.situation: Bottom of the ZT1 play screen, all times
observations.observation: One continuous horizontal strip left-to-right: Pause/Resume, Current Date, Available Cash, Zoo Status button (with inline mini status-bar), Animal List button (with inline happiness bar), Guest List button (with inline happiness bar), Staff List button (with inline happiness bar). Each roster button carries its own short colored meter fused onto the button itself, not in a separate readout.
observations.designLesson: Collapsing 'which roster' + 'how healthy is that roster' into one compact button+meter unit is very information-dense for its footprint.
observations.transfers: A left people-rail icon-button can carry an inline mini-meter (e.g. morale) the same way, answering roster health without opening it.
observations.doesNotTransfer: ZT1 fuses unrelated data (clock, money, three rosters) into one undifferentiated strip with only spacing as grouping; a 2D lot HUD with dedicated rails should keep rail-specific status visually separate from global economy status.

observations.situation: Clicking an individual animal, guest, or staff member
observations.observation: All three entity types open the same structural card: name field top-left, a row of action-icon buttons beneath the name (track/move/fire/etc.), and a vertical stack of labeled meter bars, differing only in which tabs are present (Animal/Guest: Status-General-Thoughts; Staff: Status-Job Assignment).
observations.designLesson: One reusable 'selected-entity card' component scales across very different entity types with only content swapped, which is a strong componentization precedent.
observations.transfers: One selected-person/selected-project card template can serve both a people-rail click and a pictures/lot click, keeping the player's mental model consistent across rails.
observations.doesNotTransfer: ZT1's card is a thin floating palette window with only a tiny circular portrait icon; don't copy the visual thinness — a modern card should carry a real illustrated portrait.

observations.situation: Guest happiness bar and exhibit fence-condition icon
observations.observation: Manual states the guest happiness bar turns yellow for 'unhappy' and red for 'angry'; the exhibit fence icon is green when the fence is in good condition, yellow when in bad condition, and red when a segment has been worn away or trampled. Other meters (happiness, hunger, health, exhibit suitability in the Animal panel) are depicted as plain green bars of varying length with no stated color-state language.
observations.designLesson: A green-yellow-red ramp is reserved for genuine problem states (guest anger, fence failure) rather than applied to every meter.
observations.transfers: Reserve red/yellow strictly for attention-worthy alerts (a project at risk, a burned-out staffer) so color keeps its urgency signal; routine stats can be length-only bars.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Don't color-code every meter in a busier modern HUD — ZT1's restraint is the lesson, not an invitation to add more color states.

observations.situation: Any time an info/construction panel is open
observations.observation: A fixed lower-left diamond minimap with its own independent zoom, rotate, and camera-snapshot controls persists regardless of which info or construction panel is open; panels are described and diagrammed as adjacent floating windows, not full-screen takeovers of the 3D view.
observations.designLesson: Contextual, non-modal panels plus an always-present minimap preserve the player's spatial orientation while managing rosters.
observations.transfers: Dock rail panels beside the central lot rather than over it, and keep a wayfinding element (minimap or equivalent) visible at all times regardless of what panel is open.

observations.situation: ZT2 camera/mode system, hotkeys G and C
observations.observation: ZT2 adds 'Zoo Guest Mode' (first-person, walk around, care for animals as a zookeeper) and 'Photo Safari Mode' as hotkeyed, button-accessible peers of Overview Map and Overhead View in the main button schematic. Team Zoo manual text frames guest mode explicitly as optional flavor ('even the busiest zoo tycoons take time to drop into Zoo Guest Mode'), not a requirement for management tasks.
observations.designLesson: A deliberate, cheap 'drop into the world' camera mode can sit as a sibling of the top-down management view without becoming a separate game.
observations.transfers: An optional 'walk the lot'/cinematic camera toggle for a 2D or isometric studio sim can be pure flavor, built cheaply, without touching the core management loop.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Never make this mode load-bearing for status information — in ZT2 all real management (rosters, construction, staff assignment) stays available in the top-down/panel mode; a modern HUD should resist burying functional info inside an immersive camera mode.

observations.situation: ZT2 main screen chrome, 'Main Game Buttons' schematic
observations.observation: Three visually distinct control tiers: an upper 2x4 grid of small square 'meta' utility icons (quick stats, finances, undo, recycle, goals, photo album, fame, save/load/exit), a lower row of 4 large circular mode-select buttons (Construction/Animals/Landscaping/Staff) plus rotate/zoom controls, and a separate vertical left-edge strip of small show/hide visibility-toggle icons (guests, buildings, fences, foliage, emoticons, view area, elevated path, show timer).
observations.designLesson: Separating controls into global-utility / mode-select / visibility-toggle tiers by icon shape and screen position keeps roughly 20 buttons legible without one flat toolbar.
observations.transfers: A studio HUD's left people rail and right pictures rail can each carry their own small filter/visibility strip distinct from the main rail content, mirroring this three-tier separation.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The sheer total button count (20+ visible chrome buttons) is a lot for a 2026 audience; consolidate the utility tier into fewer, denser controls (e.g. one overflow/settings menu) rather than copying the raw count.

observations.situation: Construction Panel and Animal Panel layout
observations.observation: Both catalogue panels share one two-row header grammar: a row of category tabs (Paths/Fences/Buildings/... for Construction; Adopt-Animals/Animal-Food/Toys-Enrichment/Animal-Shelters for Animals) sits above a filter-icon row, above a scrollable strip/grid of item thumbnails. Thumbnails in the manual's capture are small, flat icon-scale renders with no visible secondary stat (price, size) baked into the card.
observations.designLesson: One reusable tab-over-filter-over-grid template serves three structurally different catalogues (construction objects, animals, landscaping), aiding learnability.
observations.transfers: A right pictures-rail catalogue can reuse one tab-over-filter-over-grid template across sub-catalogues (by genre, era, or status) instead of inventing a new layout per tab.
observations.doesNotTransfer: A modern catalogue card typically needs at least one visible stat (cost, rarity, quality) baked into the thumbnail at grid density; ZT2's grid as captured does not show this, so don't copy that thinness.

observations.situation: Community modding around the base ZT2 catalogue UI
observations.observation: A third-party 'Creator's Panel' mod adds a search bar (revealed by clicking part of the filter bar) letting players find animals/objects by display name or code name, per its own description found via search — the base game's catalogue apparently had no built-in name search.
observations.designLesson: A mod built solely to add text search to the catalogue grid is circumstantial evidence that the tab-over-filter-over-grid pattern (see prior observation) stops scaling once the catalogue grows large — ZT2 Ultimate Collection's own manual advertises 100+ animals across the base game plus 4 expansions.
observations.transfers: Build search-by-name into a rail's catalogue once it is expected to exceed roughly a screen's worth of icons, rather than waiting for players to mod it in.
observations.doesNotTransfer: Low-confidence secondary-source finding; treat as directional, not as a confirmed screenshot-verified UI gap.

comp:zootycoon.summary: Gathered strong primary evidence from the official printed manuals of Zoo Tycoon (2001) and Zoo Tycoon 2: Ultimate Collection (2008 compile of the 2004 base game + 4 expansions) — both manuals contain actual annotated captures/schematics of the live UI, which were downloaded, rendered to page images, and visually inspected (not just read as text). Video and third-party screenshot-gallery evidence (YouTube, MobyGames) was blocked by the sandbox's network access in this session, so all visual observations are still-image/manual-diagram based; this is noted as a limitation but the manuals themselves are strong first-party, edition-dated sources for interface structure. Produced 8 concrete, evidence-cited observations covering: the fused status-bar+meter bottom strip (ZT1), a reusable 3-tab selected-entity card shared across animal/guest/staff (ZT1), disciplined color-as-alert-only status coding (ZT1), non-modal panels over a persistent minimap (ZT1), ZT2's added first-person Zoo Guest/Photo Safari camera modes as optional flavor siblings to the management view, ZT2's three-tier button chrome (utility/mode-select/visibility-toggle), ZT2's shared tab-over-filter-over-grid catalogue template, and a community-mod-sourced (lower-confidence) signal that the base catalogue lacked name search at scale. One review citation (GameRant 'clunky interface') was checked and found to be about an unrelated 2013 reboot by a different studio and was explicitly excluded rather than misattributed to the Blue Fang originals. All observations state what transfers and what should not transfer to a 2D studio-management HUD with a left people rail, right pictures rail, and central lot.

observations.situation: Live Mode, controlling an adult Sim in a loft apartment
observations.observation: Sims 2's persistent bottom-left cluster is a circular DIAL of small round mode-switch buttons (Needs/Personality/Relationships/etc., green=active) wrapped around a central hub, with the active Sim's rectangular head-and-shoulders portrait inset beside it, small tick-bars + name/age line under the portrait, and a separate money pill below-left. Small footprint (~1/6 screen width), fixed position, semi-transparent, world never blocked.
observations.designLesson: A fixed corner cluster can carry both 'who is selected' and 'what lens am I in' in one glanceable object, but a radial layout is not self-explanatory without hovering/learning.
observations.transfers: Fixed-corner, low-footprint status cluster that survives camera moves; pairing a portrait with compact status directly beside it.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The literal radial/dial shape reads as dated skeuomorphism and doesn't scale past a handful of panels or to touch input; use flat tabs instead.

observations.situation: Same frame as above
observations.observation: Two small square household-member portraits are stacked vertically at the far-left edge above the dial; the active one has a bright green border. Only present household members shown (2 here), implying the strip grows/shrinks with roster size rather than reserving fixed slots.
observations.designLesson: A literal column of small face-thumbnails, decoupled from the detailed per-Sim panel, keeps the whole household in peripheral view while one Sim's detail stays expanded.
observations.transfers: Small square/circular headshot column with one highlighted-border selection state, length driven by roster size — directly maps to a left people-rail.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The extreme thumbnail size (~24x24px in this capture) — modern displays can support larger, more legible cards without cost.

observations.situation: Same frame
observations.observation: A docked 'Wants' strip (green-tinted, thought-bubble icons, 4 slots) sits directly above a mirrored 'Fears' strip (red-tinted, 4 slots) beside the portrait; both stay on-screen with the world still rendering/simulating behind them.
observations.designLesson: Color-coded twin strips for near-term goals vs. risks, shown at a glance without a modal, is a strong pattern for 'what should I do next.'
observations.transfers: A docked, color-coded opportunities-vs-risks pair (e.g., a project near a milestone vs. one about to slip) in a right-rail.
observations.doesNotTransfer: The literal thought-bubble-cloud art style — dated; use plain iconography + text-on-hover instead.

observations.locator: video S2 @ 15:00, cropped from sims2_f_630.jpg/sims2_f_900 region
observations.situation: Buy Mode, placing furniture
observations.observation: Buy Mode swaps the Live-mode dial+portrait for a mode-icon cluster (same top-left corner), a category-folder picker, and a horizontally scrolling item-icon strip with color-swatch chips beneath each icon — matching the Live panel's height and dock position almost exactly; the lot stays fully visible above it.
observations.designLesson: Switching modes doesn't require switching screens; keeping the panel's dock position/height constant across modes lowers the mode-switch cost because the eye doesn't relearn where to look.
observations.transfers: Dock a catalogue/placement-mode panel in the exact same rail the default HUD occupies so the central-lot view never disappears.
observations.doesNotTransfer: A second row of color-swatch chips under each item icon — a modern icon+detail-on-select pattern reads faster.

observations.locator: video S2 @ 15:00, camera pulled to wide exterior view
observations.situation: Zooming the camera far out to see the whole building exterior
observations.observation: The bottom-left dial/portrait cluster stays exactly the same on-screen size and position as the camera zooms out; a small mini-map appears at bottom-right only at this zoom level.
observations.designLesson: The always-on HUD's footprint should stay fixed regardless of camera zoom level rather than scaling to fill unused space.
observations.transfers: Keep HUD footprint fixed across all central-lot camera zoom levels; introduce a mini-map only at wide zoom.
observations.doesNotTransfer: n/a — worth keeping as-is.

observations.situation: Live Mode, Sim on a home gym treadmill, needs panel opened
observations.observation: Six needs (Bladder, Fun, Hunger, Social, Energy, Hygiene) are shown two-per-row in a rounded white card, each with icon + text label + colored bar (green=healthy, amber/gold=low, seen on Fun here); this card only appears above the compact bottom-right icon dock on interaction — the resting/default footprint is much smaller.
observations.designLesson: Collapsing detailed numeric needs behind a one-click/hover flyout — while keeping a compact always-on icon row as default — recovers screen space without losing at-a-glance access, provided the collapsed state still shows some signal (moodlet/emotion color per S1).
observations.transfers: Default-collapsed status rail with one-interaction expand to full breakdown; row-per-metric layout (icon+label+bar).
observations.doesNotTransfer: The drop-shadowed card floating disconnected from its dock icon — should visually hinge off the rail it expands from.

observations.situation: Official Players Guide text describing the Live Mode UI
observations.observation: 'The bottom right corner of the UI contains all of the key information about who your Sim is… Traits, Skills, Relationships, Motives, Career Info, and progress against your Sim's Aspirations… you can even change your Sim's Aspiration at any time.' And: 'Your Sim's current Emotion can be seen… most importantly, in the bottom left corner of the user interface. Here you'll find information on Moodlets.'
observations.designLesson: Officially, Sims 4 splits identity/relationship/skill depth (bottom-right) from moment-to-moment emotional state (bottom-left) into two separate docked zones rather than one panel.
observations.transfers: Split a people-rail's 'who/relationships/skills' depth panel from a separate compact 'current state/alert' zone.
observations.doesNotTransfer: n/a

observations.situation: Same frame as needs panel above
observations.observation: The active Sim's circular portrait sits inside a colored glow/ring (green, keyed to current emotion) with two thought-bubble interaction icons above it, and a second smaller portrait (queued interaction target) plus two small action-queue icons docked directly beneath it — identity, emotion, and interaction queue fused into one cluster, denser than Sims 2's plain rectangular headshot.
observations.designLesson: A portrait that also encodes state via a colored ring removes the need for a separate mood readout, at the cost of requiring the player to learn a color code.
observations.transfers: Colored ring/glow around a person-card portrait to encode one high-priority status (overworked/blocked/on-track).
observations.doesNotTransfer: Nesting a full interaction queue as tiny icons inside the portrait — likely illegible in a flat 2D isometric HUD; keep the queue as its own list element.

observations.situation: Official Players Guide controls reference
observations.observation: Verbatim: 'Switch to next Sim in household — Spacebar/N'; 'Switch to specific Sim — Click Sim portrait'; 'Lock camera to Sim — Right-click Sim portrait'; 'Center camera on active Sim — Enter.'
observations.designLesson: Left-click and right-click on the same portrait object do two distinct, non-overlapping things (select vs. camera-lock), plus an independent keyboard cycle exists — the rail doesn't need extra buttons for 'follow this person.'
observations.transfers: Left-click a person-card = select/focus; right-click = lock camera/view to that person; keyboard shortcut to cycle without touching the rail.
observations.doesNotTransfer: n/a — compact, well-generalizable convention worth keeping.
